data.title: Riskified launches AI agent identity checks for merchants
data.ai_summary: Riskified launched Agent Identity Risk Intelligence to identify the person behind AI personal assistants in online shopping and customer service. UK research found 37.9% of British shoppers would use an AI agent for refund complaints and 23.4% for chargebacks. The system will first deploy for Shopify merchants using Meta's Muse.
data.author: Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin

industries.name: Fraud Detection & Prevention (payments fraud, account takeover, scams)
Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)

data.full_text:
JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor

Riskified has launched Agent Identity Risk Intelligence for merchants dealing with AI personal assistants in online shopping and customer service. The product is designed to identify the person behind an AI agent and return a real-time risk signal. The launch comes as consumer AI assistants begin placing orders, filing claims, seeking refunds and handling returns on behalf of shoppers. That creates a new challenge for retailers, which have traditionally relied on device, browser and account signals to detect fraud. The new offering extends Riskified's existing identity risk tools to interactions initiated by personal AI agents such as Meta's Muse, Instinct and similar services. It is designed to recognise when an order or service request comes from an AI assistant, link that request to the underlying consumer identity and assess whether the activity should be trusted. That reflects a shift in how merchants may need to view automated activity online. In the past, signals such as a single-use card, relay email address or lack of device history could indicate suspicious behaviour. With AI agents acting for legitimate customers, those same signals may no longer be enough to separate fraud from authorised delegation. Riskified's UK research points to early consumer interest in using such tools for post-purchase disputes. It said 37.9% of British shoppers would use an AI agent to draft a refund or credit complaint, while 23.4% would use one to initiate a bank chargeback if a return proved difficult. New risk model For merchants, the issue is moving beyond whether an interaction is automated to whether the automation has been authorised by a legitimate and trustworthy person. Riskified argued that newer standards for agent verification may confirm that an assistant has permission to act, but do not in themselves address whether the underlying account holder is genuine or whether the request is part of a fraud scheme. That distinction matters because an authorised agent could still be linked to account takeover, fake accounts or organised refund abuse. The system is intended to sit alongside emerging agent protocols by focusing on the identity of the person who granted the authority. "Agent protocols solve a real problem: merchants need a secure way to let a customer's assistant act for them. What they don't solve is whether that customer should be trusted. A fraud ring can authorize an agent as easily as a loyal shopper can," said Assaf Feldman, Chief Strategy Officer, Technology and Co-Founder at Riskified. "Riskified sits on top of those protocols and answers the harder question, using what our identity engine already knows about the person behind the agent, so merchants can welcome a good customer's assistant, decline a bad actor's, and notice the moment a real customer's agent starts doing something that the customer never would," Feldman said. Checkout to claims The product covers both checkout and post-purchase interactions. When standard device and browser telemetry is missing, as can happen when an AI assistant acts for a shopper, the system relies more heavily on identity records, network history and the behaviour of the agent itself. For refund and return interactions, it can engage directly with the assistant to confirm details or apply additional checks. The approach is intended to distinguish between a legitimate assistant acting for a real customer and a scripted process used by fraudsters. The first deployment will focus on merchants using Shopify, where orders placed through Meta's Muse already arrive marked as agent-originated, according to Riskified. Coverage will expand to other commerce platforms as standards for identifying agents become more widely adopted. Alongside the core launch, Riskified will support policy controls by agent type in its Decision Studio product. That would allow merchants, for example, to approve lower-risk agent orders tied to verified identities while sending higher-risk refund claims for review. The same risk category will also feed into the company's Zendesk integration, giving both human support staff and AI service agents visibility when a refund or return request comes through a consumer AI assistant. Fraud concerns The broader concern for retailers is that tools designed to help consumers manage shopping and after-sales service could also make organised abuse easier to scale. Riskified pointed to refund fraud groups that already use scripted claims involving missing items or empty boxes against large retailers. It argued that persistent AI agents could increase the volume and frequency of such activity by allowing bad actors to automate repetitive tasks across orders and support channels. In that environment, merchants may need fraud systems that assess both the source of the automated request and the identity behind it. Reporting on agent-originated traffic will be added to Riskified's Control Centre, including approval rates, fraud rates and claim abuse rates, with breakdowns by assistant where that information is available. The company said the data would help merchants compare the performance of agent-driven activity with the rest of their business. Agent Identity Risk Intelligence will be available through Riskified's existing APIs and its AI Agent Approve MCP server on AWS Marketplace.

data.title: Data takes center stage as 1,000 tech professionals gather at Tel Aviv AI conference
data.ai_summary: Over 1,000 data professionals gathered in Tel Aviv for the sixth hayaData conference, organized by Riskified, to discuss AI and data infrastructure. JLL forecasts nearly $3 trillion in data center investment by 2030, and IDC data shows 90% of global data generated in the past two years.
data.author: Ynet Global

industries.name: AI Datacenter Power, Cooling & Racks (liquid cooling, power delivery)

data.full_text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
More than 1,000 data professionals gathered in Tel Aviv for the sixth annual hayaData conference, bringing together executives and experts from some of the world's largest technology companies to discuss the growing role of artificial intelligence, data infrastructure and automation in the global economy.
The conference, held at the David InterContinental Hotel, is organized by Israeli fraud prevention company Riskified as a nonprofit community initiative. It features dozens of speakers from companies including Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google, Wix, NVIDIA, Microsoft, monday.com, Databricks, Snowflake, HoneyBook, Cato Networks and AI21 Labs.
The event comes as demand for data processing and storage continues to accelerate, driven largely by the expansion of AI technologies and the infrastructure needed to support them.
According to real estate services firm JLL's 2026 forecast, the global data center industry will require nearly $3 trillion in investment by 2030 to accommodate approximately 100 gigawatts of additional capacity, effectively doubling the sector's existing capacity.
The expansion is expected to place growing pressure on electricity grids and increase demand for innovative energy solutions. JLL projects the sector will grow at a compound annual rate of 14%, with major technology companies expanding their computing infrastructure through a combination of leased data centers and facilities they develop themselves.
'A foundational infrastructure reshaping the rules'
Noa Lubin, CTO at the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office, emphasized the strategic importance of artificial intelligence to Israel's economy and national security.
"Artificial intelligence isn't just technology — it's a foundational infrastructure reshaping the rules of business, society and geopolitics," Lubin said.
"Leadership and sovereignty in this field are vital prerequisites for Israel's national strength."
The growing importance of AI has placed renewed emphasis on the enormous quantities of information required to train, operate and improve advanced computing systems.
According to IDC figures cited by conference organizers, roughly 90% of the world's data was generated within the past two years, while global data storage volumes approximately double every four years.
The rapid growth presents challenges for companies seeking to process information efficiently while maintaining accuracy, security and reliability.
Guy Machlev, vice president of research and development at Riskified, said the proliferation of AI-powered systems capable of acting independently has made reliable data more important than ever.
"The data landscape is at a critical turning point," Machlev said. "The AI revolution doesn't lessen the importance of data — it makes it more critical than ever."
He said the industry was moving beyond traditional systems that primarily analyze information toward a new generation of autonomous AI agents capable of making decisions and performing tasks on behalf of users.
"We are moving from systems that primarily analyze information to an era where AI agents make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users," he said.
"This shift introduces new challenges in trust, identity and risk management, underscoring the vital need for high-quality data and precise, real-time decision-making."
Machlev said Riskified's own operations illustrated the scale of the transformation.
"Over the past five years, the volume of data we process at Riskified has grown more than fivefold, accompanied by significant improvements in processing speed and efficiency," he said.
"These capabilities serve as the foundation for navigating the new challenges of the agentic AI era."
Agentic AI refers to artificial intelligence systems designed to pursue goals and carry out sequences of tasks with varying degrees of autonomy, rather than simply responding to individual prompts.
The technology is expected to expand the range of activities that companies can automate, while creating new challenges involving accountability, fraud prevention and the verification of automated decisions.
AI transforms the skills required of data professionals
Beyond the infrastructure challenges, conference participants also examined how AI is changing the responsibilities and expertise required of employees working with data.
Amit BenDor, head of AI and data science at Unity, said increasingly accessible AI tools were enabling employees without specialized technical training to perform tasks traditionally reserved for data professionals.
"The data space is evolving rapidly, and AI is redefining job roles, scope of responsibility and the skill sets required for professionals," BenDor said.
"On one hand, more people across various roles can now build dashboards and execute tasks that once demanded dedicated expertise."
He said the democratization of data tools did not eliminate the need for specialists but instead shifted the emphasis toward deeper analytical judgment and the ability to use AI effectively.
"Because of this democratization, two types of expertise become critical," BenDor said.
The first, he explained, is deep knowledge of a particular field, including the ability to identify underlying problems, formulate relevant questions and draw meaningful conclusions beyond superficial findings.
The second is proficiency in applying AI tools across the data ecosystem, including analytics, data engineering and data science.
The changes reflect a broader shift in how companies organize their technical teams, as AI increasingly automates routine data processing and analysis while placing greater value on problem-solving and domain expertise.
More than 50 sessions across four tracks
The hayaData conference aims to provide Israel's data community with practical knowledge drawn from real-world industry experience, allowing participants to explore emerging technologies, methodologies and frameworks they can apply in their daily work.
The program includes more than 50 technical presentations and sessions organized into four tracks: Data Engineering, Data Science, Analytics and Business Intelligence, and Data Products.
This year's event places particular emphasis on the intersection of data and artificial intelligence, examining how AI is transforming the way organizations collect, build, manage and use information.
Sessions also address the changing roles of data professionals as companies increasingly integrate AI into their operations.
The gathering reflects the growing importance of data not only as a resource for businesses but also as a foundation for technological innovation and national competitiveness, with governments and private companies investing heavily in the infrastructure, expertise and computing power needed to participate in the expanding AI economy.

data.title: Riskified: New Merchants Bring Growth And Margin Pressure (NYSE:RSKD)
data.ai_summary: Riskified reported Q2 revenue of $98.7 million, up 22% year-over-year, but gross margin fell to 46% from 52% as new merchants drove growth. The company raised its adjusted EBITDA guidance to $33-$39 million, but margin compression continues into Q3. The stock trades at 33.8 times FY1 non-GAAP earnings, and the author rates it a Hold.
data.author: Daniel James

industries.name: Fraud Detection & Prevention (payments fraud, account takeover, scams)

data.full_text:
Introduction
Riskified (RSKD), an e-commerce fraud prevention and risk management platform powered by AI, has seen its growth pick up considerably this year. Revenue growth in the second quarter increased to 22%, up from 7% during the first quarter, and consensus expects double digit revenue growth to continue into 2027. However, the recent growth spurt comes with a catch. New merchant additions are driving much of the acceleration, and they initially generate lower margins, which means that gross profit growth has not kept pace with sales growth. Meanwhile, the valuation is fairly high at around 34 times forward non-GAAP earnings, and the stock is already up nearly 77% over the past year. This is cause for me to remain cautious until the company shows clearer evidence of margin improvement.
New Merchants Are Driving Growth
During the second quarter, revenue hit $98.7 million for a 22% year-over-year increase, up from 7% in the first quarter. Much of this growth was attributed to new customers and existing merchants expanding their business. Digital finance was by far the fastest-growing category with 180% growth, driven by several newly launched merchants in event contracts and gaming. However, it's unclear how much the category contributed to overall revenue growth.
Growth in tickets and travel also accelerated, up to around 23% versus 18% in the first quarter. Growth was led by ticketing, aided by higher activity among major existing customers. The events calendar did provide a boost, with both the World Cup and NBA Finals leading to higher transaction volumes. Travel grew as well, but management described the growth as softer than earlier in the year.
The number of merchants using multiple products was up by around 50% year-over-year, while management expects net dollar retention to remain around 105%. It's encouraging that existing merchants are buying more products, but the current growth acceleration still relies heavily on signing up new merchants. The key question then becomes whether the company can sustain new customer additions as the boost from major sporting events fades.
Higher Revenue Isn't Translating Into the Same Profit Growth
The company's accelerated revenue growth came at a cost, with revenue growth outpacing gross profit growth for the quarter. Non-GAAP gross profit was up by 13% against a 22% increase in revenue, as non-GAAP gross margin decreased to 46% from the 52% reported in the first quarter.
According to management, the margin pressure was due to two main changes in the business mix. Firstly, new merchants usually start at lower margins. Secondly, ticketing, which generally has lower margins anyway, contributed more to the overall business. This doesn't look like evidence of broader deterioration as existing merchants continued to perform well, according to management.
Newer business apparently also had a higher risk profile, which would explain the higher implied fee rate during the quarter. Fortunately, management does expect newer customer groups to become more profitable over time, but no timeline was provided for this. This is definitely something to keep an eye on going into upcoming earnings. The outlook for Q3 suggests that the gap will continue, with management expecting 27% revenue growth and gross profit growth closer to the 13% delivered in Q2. This implies further margin compression.
This is not to say that the company's strategy is wrong. New merchants can support future earnings growth even with lower initial margins. However, without numbers or a clear timeline, it's hard to judge when margins will recover.
Higher Profit Targets and Heavy Buybacks
Despite the pressure on gross margin, the company raised its adjusted EBITDA guidance for the year to $33-$39 million, up from an earlier range of $28-$34 million. At the midpoint, this is an increase of about 16% and implies an adjusted EBITDA margin of around 8.9%.
Central to reaching that target is discipline with regard to operating expenses, which we can already see showing up in the numbers. Non-GAAP operating expenses in Q2 came in at $41.5 million, or 42% of revenue, versus 47% a year ago. The company expects quarterly expenses of $42-$43 million, so if it can keep growing gross profit while expenses remain roughly around the Q2 level, more gross profit can flow into earnings.
However, guidance requires a much stronger second half of the year. Adjusted EBITDA during the first half of the year was around $10.1 million, so the company needs to earn $25.9 million during the second half, or roughly 2.6 times what it did during the first half.
Meanwhile, the company is buying back stock fairly aggressively, with the Q2 repurchase consideration roughly 4.9 times quarterly free cash flow. This means the company is drawing on existing liquidity to buy back shares. While a lower share count can support future EPS, it doesn't automatically create value.
The Valuation Already Assumes Better Profitability
Riskified trades at around 33.8 times FY1 non-GAAP earnings and 22.2 times FY2 earnings. Of course, the lower multiple for FY2 assumes the company will achieve the expected earnings increase, which is asking quite a lot. EPS is expected to rise by nearly 52% between 2026 and 2027 on a revenue increase of only 11.2%. This means the company needs either considerably better profitability and/or considerably fewer shares outstanding.
Riskified also looks fairly expensive in terms of forward EV/EBITDA at 25.82 times versus a sector median of 14 times, although the forward price to sales of 2.8 is a bit of a discount to the 3.34 times sector median. Its forward EV/sales are also around 34% above its own five-year average.
Conclusion
It's not hard to see why investors like Riskified. The company is growing revenue quickly as new merchants drive expansion, and the company raised its annual revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. However, margins remain under pressure as newer merchants typically have lower profitability, and no timetable was given for a recovery in margins. Expectations are high going into 2027, and the company's valuation currently assumes that little will go wrong. Until the company can demonstrate continued customer additions together with improving gross margins and can deliver on the higher profit targets, I rate Riskified a Hold.

data.title: Announcing a specialized AI agent designed to meet business needs.
data.ai_summary: Zendesk announced the launch of Specialized Agents, including an Industry-Specific Agent for retail and a Custom Agent, which autonomously handle up to 80% of business operations. The MCP Client is now generally available in Japan, and early access programs are running with formal support planned later this year.

industries.name: Workplace Automation & Self-Service (RPA for IT, Chatbots, Virtual Agents)
Agents & Autonomous Workflows (Tool Use, Planning, Multi-Agent)
Customer Service/Support CRM & Contact Center Platforms

data.full_text: Zendesk LLC (Headquarters: Chuo-ku, Tokyo, Representative Executive Officer: Taro Mori, hereinafter "Zendesk") announced today the launch of "Specialized Agents," designed to optimize operations that are highly important for specific companies and industries. By integrating industry-specific expertise, unique knowledge from each company, and existing workflows and collaboration systems, it autonomously handles up to 80% of business operations (*). Additionally, it was announced that the general availability of "MCP Client" has begun in Japan. This announcement includes a retail version of the "Industry-Specific Agent" that addresses key common operations in specific industries, as well as a "Custom Agent" built based on each company's unique processes and policies. By utilizing both functions, organizations can entrust many processes across all business workflows to AI. The Specialized Agent is an important step towards the "Autonomous Service Workforce" first announced at Zendesk's annual event Relate 2026 held in May. It is based on a clear vision where AI automatically executes many operations while companies maintain control over the processes. l "Industry-Specific AI Agent" with immediate industry expertise The "Industry-Specific AI Agent" has been developed to address key common operations in specific industries. It will initially be available for the retail industry, where the AI agent will support all aspects of purchasing, including order management, returns and exchanges, delivery issues, and refund processing. In the future, Zendesk plans to expand the industry-specific agents to a wide range of industries such as financial services, media, and technology, bringing industry-specific expertise into daily operations. The Industry-Specific AI Agent integrates necessary systems, operational policies, and specialized knowledge with Zendesk AI to complete high-priority business processes end-to-end. For the retail industry, it will collaborate with major systems such as Shopify, Narvar, Stripe, and Riskified to understand customer requests, extract appropriate information, and autonomously execute actions. This will eliminate the hassle of customers and support staff switching between multiple systems. Furthermore, in partnership with Riskified, it directly integrates top-class risk intelligence into e-commerce business processes. This reduces the risk of fraud and unjust claims while enabling retail businesses to make smarter decisions regarding returns, refunds, and exchanges. The Industry-Specific AI Agent is expected to launch an early access program soon, with Japanese support available at the time of general release, planned for later this year. l "Custom Agent" tailored to unique business operations Each company has its own operational rules, approval procedures, and unique business processes, so it is not possible to cover all business processes with packaged standard functions alone. By utilizing the "Agent Builder," which allows for no-code construction, testing, and deployment of agents, companies can build "Custom Agents" tailored to their operations. The early access program has already been executed over a million times within seven weeks, with reports of a 10% increase in the rate of automatic resolution after implementation. Companies can define the scope of operations handled by the AI agent, the systems available for use, the actions that can be executed, and the situations that require human approval. Additionally, the AI agent can proactively operate according to business events and schedules, achieving extensive automation beyond just responding to customer inquiries. The early access program for the Custom Agent has already started and operates in Japanese, with formal support planned for general release later this year. l An integrated "Workforce" that functions across all service platforms Both the "Industry-Specific AI Agent" and the "Custom Agent" can operate on existing service environments, including Salesforce and ServiceNow, in addition to Zendesk. Companies can implement and utilize specialized AI agents without switching their currently used systems. Furthermore, the general availability of the MCP Client is also announced today. By utilizing the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Zendesk's AI agents and Copilot can accurately obtain necessary real-time data beyond the confines of isolated language models from existing systems. This enhances the accuracy of AI and brings better results for both support staff and customers. As AI agents complete more tasks, Zendesk will continuously learn from the results. By visualizing success factors, points where support was needed, and future improvement measures, it will support the continuous improvement of service quality within organizations. 【Comment】 Shashi Upadhyay, President of Products, Engineering, and AI at Zendesk "The era of generic and uniform AI agents is over. Truly excellent support staff are specialists deeply rooted in specific operations, industries, and individual businesses. Specialized AI agents provide the expertise and context necessary to address more complex operations, enabling organizations to build trust and achieve quantitative results." For more details, please see below. Blog: https://www.zendesk.co.jp/blog/zendesk-insights/innovation/specialized-agents-are-here/ Website: https://www.zendesk.co.jp/service/ai/ai-agents/specialized-agents/ *According to Zendesk's internal research About Zendesk Zendesk leads the autonomous service workforce powered by AI agents, automation, and human expertise. It harmonizes all support experiences across all operational settings, focusing on personal, meaningful solutions without interruption. Our Zendesk Resolution Platform integrates the power of organizations into a single platform that is enhanced through all interactions. Zendesk uses AI as a means to consistently seek concrete results and values lasting relationships. Based on this philosophy, we aim for organizations to provide high-quality support while customers and employees can enjoy it. For more information, please visit https://www.zendesk.co.jp/.

data.full_text:
A 10.8% rise in the share price of Riskified (NYSE: RSKD) last Thursday brought it to its highest level since the end of 2021. On Friday, the stock weakened a little, but the company still ended the week with a market cap above $1 billion for the first time in a long time.
Riskified is a fintech company that provides a solution for the prevention of fraud in ecommerce. The company, headed by co-founder Eido Gal, was floated on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, a boom year for flotations, at a valuation of $3.3 billion, which it has never seen since.
Riskified did not release any report last week that might explain the jump in its share price. On investment website Zacks, it was stated that Riskified was enjoying growing demand arising from the fact that incidents of fraud were becoming more complicated.
In its second quarter financials released last month, Riskified reported its fastest growth in revenue in recent years, by 22% to $98.7 million. It posted a net loss of $9.1 million, which represents an improvement over the corresponding quarter, and positive EBITDA of $3.9 million.
Riskified expects revenue for 2026 to total $400-410 million and EBITDA for the year of $33-39 million. The mid-point of the guidance represents growth of 17.5% in revenue and 34.7% in EBITDA in comparison with 2025.

Zendesk Unveils Specialized AI Agents to Transform Business Workflows Small businesses face numerous challenges in delivering efficient customer service while also managing operational costs. A recent announcement from Zendesk promises a potential game-changer for these enterprises. The company has introduced Specialized AI Agents, designed specifically to align with the unique workflows of different businesses and industries. These tools aim to automate up to 80% of workflows, offering small business owners a powerful resource to enhance their operations. Zendesk’s Specialized AI Agents come in two flavors: Industry Agents and Custom Agents. The Industry Agents are preconfigured for specific sectors, such as commerce, allowing businesses to quickly implement AI-driven solutions without extensive customization. For example, a retail business could leverage these agents to assist customers in shopping, managing orders, and resolving common issues related to returns and refunds. Custom Agents, on the other hand, allow businesses to build AI solutions tailored to their unique processes and requirements using Zendesk’s no-code environment, known as Agent Builder. Shashi Upadhyay, Zendesk’s President of Product, Engineering, and AI, stated, “The era of generic, one-size-fits-all AI agents is over. The best agents are specialists: deeply grounded in the work, the industry, and the business they serve.” This shift towards specialization could help small businesses tackle more complex tasks traditionally handled by human employees, reducing bottlenecks and wait times for customers, and accelerating operational efficiencies. Small businesses that implement these Specialized Agents could see a significant improvement in service speed and quality. For instance, the integration of agents with platforms like Shopify, Narvar, and Stripe allows for seamless management of orders and customer inquiries, reducing the need for human intervention. This could be particularly beneficial for e-commerce businesses where quick response times can enhance customer satisfaction and potentially increase sales. In addition to improving customer experiences, the platform offers significant benefits in risk management. For example, Zendesk has partnered with Riskified, a leader in risk intelligence, to embed risk assessment directly into commerce workflows. This feature can help retailers minimize fraud-related losses while providing a smoother and more secure transaction experience for legitimate customers. Jeff Otto, Chief Marketing Officer of Riskified, commented, “Zendesk Industry Agents are the AI-first platform redefining retail service at scale.” While the potential benefits are considerable, small business owners should also consider several challenges that may accompany the adoption of AI-driven solutions. Transitioning to a system that utilizes Specialized AI Agents may require an initial investment of time and resources. Business owners must ensure they have the necessary infrastructure in place to support these tools, including adequate employee training and integration with existing systems. Moreover, even though the no-code Agent Builder aims to simplify customization, there may still be a learning curve. Owners will need to determine how best to configure agents to fit their specific operational needs, potentially requiring ongoing adjustments as business processes evolve. It’s essential for entrepreneurs to continuously monitor AI performance, ensuring that service quality stays high and that AI delivers the expected results without compromising the personalized customer care that many small businesses pride themselves on. In a marketplace that increasingly prioritizes customer experience, adopting Specialized AI Agents could offer small businesses a competitive edge. As these AI tools evolve, they promise to take on more complex work, allowing business owners to focus on strategic initiatives rather than getting bogged down in routine tasks. Thus, for small business owners considering integrating AI into their operations, Zendesk’s Specialized AI Agents may represent an opportunity to streamline processes, enhance customer satisfaction, and ultimately drive growth. data.ai_summary: Polymarket's US betting platform faced a fraud attack in February where criminals used stolen debit cards to deposit and withdraw funds, with over 80% of deposits fraudulent. industries.name: Fraud Detection & Prevention (payments fraud, account takeover, scams)

data.full_text: Authors: Katherine Long, Caitlin Ostroff, Neil Mehta Compiled by: Chopper, Foresight News In February of this year, a warning message came from a partner handling debit card transactions for Polymarket's US betting platform: a large number of fraudsters flooded the platform. Criminals linked stolen debit cards to Polymarket US accounts, used the accounts to place bets, and then attempted to withdraw the funds to clean bank cards or accounts they controlled, trying to abscond with at least $10 million. During the incident, the payment institution determined that over 80% of deposit transactions were fraudulent, a rate far higher than the industry standard of about 1%. Insiders said that Polymarket employees immediately reported this risk to CEO Shayne Coplan. The compliance team recalled that Coplan's response shocked them: just continue to expand, and if regulators find issues, we can just pay fines. Current and former employees of Polymarket stated that this previously unreported statement was Coplan's business philosophy for Polymarket - pursuing growth at all costs. Current and former employees and investors interviewed by The Wall Street Journal said that this booming company was fully engaged in attracting new users and investors, during which compliance loopholes, legal disputes, and software failures occurred one after another. Insiders said that after the February attack, although the platform's fraud rate did not reach 80% again, it remained high for several months. After the incident, several executives left, and the company initiated an internal investigation. Former regulators from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the Department of Justice, and the IRS said that the extent of the attempted fraud and Polymarket's response were rare in the commodities and gambling industries. Unlike traditional commodity exchanges, Polymarket directly accepts retail funds, making it more susceptible to fraud attacks. Former CFTC enforcement lawyer Joe Konizeski stated: "In regulated areas, such things do not happen. Professionals manage client funds to ensure that the sources and disposal of funds comply with regulations." A Polymarket spokesperson stated that the company is committed to maintaining an accurate, fair, and transparent market and actively cooperating with regulatory agencies and law enforcement. "Our market integrity mechanisms include processes for detecting, verifying, and addressing suspicious activities." Polymarket is facing an increasing number of legal lawsuits on multiple fronts. The CFTC has initiated a lawsuit against it, and insiders revealed that the company has notified employees to retain records related to this fraud attack and other matters. The New York City Council is conducting a broad investigation into Polymarket and other prediction market platforms, with nearly twenty traders filing lawsuits accusing Polymarket of deceptive business practices. Meanwhile, more than a dozen state-level lawsuits focus on a core issue: whether Polymarket and its competitors like Kalshi are unlicensed gambling platforms. The rulings in these cases could reshape the entire industry landscape. Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan has urged employees to maintain the company's rapid growth pace. As legal risks continue to accumulate, Coplan is pushing for a $1 billion financing round, which, upon completion, will value the company at approximately $21 billion. Donald Trump's investment fund, 1789 Capital, will participate in this round of investment, having previously invested about $200 million in Polymarket. Polymarket has a data partnership with Dow Jones, the parent company of The Wall Street Journal. Currently, the company is working to reshape its image to investors and the public, aiming to become a mature enterprise pursuing steady growth. Insiders revealed that since May, the company has been gradually hiring experienced risk control personnel, including a former FBI agent, while improving compliance processes and optimizing product testing. Insiders said that at the end of June, Coplan visited the Hamptons residence of Omeed Malik, co-founder of 1789 Capital, to discuss strategies for improving Polymarket's internal operations before a potential IPO next year. Malik suggested that Coplan hire more senior executives. Recently, Polymarket appointed its first CFO, Warren Jenson, who previously served as CFO of Amazon in the early 2000s. After The Wall Street Journal published an investigative report on Polymarket's social media betting business, the company restructured its marketing team and hired the founder of electric scooter company Bird as the head of growth. Other marketing employees involved in the social media marketing project have either left or had their job responsibilities reduced. A company spokesperson stated: "Polymarket is rapidly developing and improving every day. We are proud of our newly appointed core management team and the continuously upgraded infrastructure. In the forefront of finance, technology, and culture, we have achieved business scaling while adhering to responsible growth." 28-year-old Coplan is known for being outspoken and assertive, having previously reprimanded employees in the office. Former employees stated that staff generally needed to work overtime and that taking Adderall (a central nervous system stimulant) was quite common within the company. Multiple former employees indicated that Coplan constantly urged engineers to iterate on new feature lists, with frequent changes in requirements. A recording reviewed by The Wall Street Journal shows that last July, during a discussion on how to adjudicate betting disputes, Coplan bluntly stated: "Dude, this is just stupid! You guys keep complaining about this, it's ridiculous." As early as 2022, after reaching a settlement with federal regulators, Polymarket was prohibited from opening its international platform to users in the US. In 2024, as Polymarket's visibility increased, two federal agencies began investigations to verify whether the company violated the settlement agreement by allowing US traders to log into the platform. Around the same time, a prankster employee in the office set up a life-sized cardboard cutout of the incarcerated crypto scammer Sam Bankman-Fried, partly as a joke due to the resemblance between Coplan, a billionaire in the crypto industry, and Sam Bankman-Fried. Last summer, the company spent $112 million to acquire a licensed exchange, transforming it into Polymarket US. Polymarket US opened to early users in December. Insiders said that a large number of traders flooded the platform, with total account deposits exceeding $500 million. As one of the anti-money laundering measures, Polymarket US adopted the common rules of financial exchanges: funds deposited from a certain payment channel must be withdrawn back to that channel. Without this rule, criminals could use stolen debit cards to recharge, complete transactions, and withdraw profits to clean bank cards. Although this application is still in beta testing and only open to a limited number of users, Coplan hopes to eliminate user experience friction as much as possible. Staff explained to users that funds were being processed, but compliance reviews could delay withdrawals by several days or even weeks. Engineering failures in the US application further exacerbated the withdrawal issue. Before the New York City mayoral election in November 2025, Polymarket's advertisements appeared on the streets of New York. Executives believed that existing protective mechanisms were sufficient to mitigate risks. When engineers raised objections and suggested prioritizing fixing existing platform vulnerabilities, Coplan sometimes instructed engineers to directly use AI to develop new features. Insiders said that LeBron James's team had previously revealed to a competitor in the prediction market that Polymarket's offer was $20 million per year plus $50 million in equity. Polymarket spokespersons and Drake's team stated that the two sides ultimately did not sign a contract. However, Drake later mentioned Polymarket and Coplan in his album "Iceman." "Polymarket US has had no response for several weeks." After he submitted identity verification materials twice, the platform froze his account, without mentioning the issue of lost funds.

Polymarket employees reportedly warned that scrapping this rule would increase money laundering risks. Leadership removed it anyway. The February 2026 attack exploited exactly the kind of vulnerability that the same-source rule was designed to prevent. Polymarket Faces Alleged $10M Stolen-Card Fraud; CFTC Said to Investigate

Polymarket US, the federally regulated prediction market operated by QCX LLC, became the target of a stolen debit-card scheme in February that involved at least $10 million in attempted illicit withdrawals and wagers, according to a Sept. 19 report by The Wall Street Journal. Polymarket US, the federally regulated prediction market operated by QCX LLC, became the target of a stolen debit-card scheme in February that involved at least $10 million in attempted illicit withdrawals and wagers, according to a Sept. 19 report by The Wall Street Journal. The $10 million figure refers to the attempted movement of funds rather than a confirmed loss suffered by customers or the company, the Journal reported. Criminals allegedly connected stolen cards to thousands of Polymarket US accounts, funded those accounts, attempted to move the money through trading, and then sought to withdraw it to cards or accounts they controlled. Polymarket US operates through QCX, which the Commodity Futures Trading Commission lists as a designated contract market and which received its designation in July 2025, according to the agency's register. Prediction markets have drawn increasing regulatory attention since the 2024 election, when Polymarket projected that Donald Trump had a 59.7% chance of winning the presidency and carried more than $584 million in bets on that outcome [1]. The State Department later issued a memorandum reminding employees worldwide that using undisclosed official information for financial gain is a "very serious offense," a directive that referenced prediction platforms including Polymarket [2]. Report: Checkout.com Rejected More Than 80% of Deposits as Fraudulent at Peak At the peak of the February attack, payment processor Checkout.com rejected more than 80% of the deposits it handled for Polymarket as fraudulent, compared with an industry level of roughly 1%. The 80% figure has not been publicly confirmed by Checkout.com in a statement reviewed for the report. The processor does provide merchants with fraud-scoring, transaction-filtering and authentication tools, and its current service terms state that merchants remain responsible for deciding whether transactions are accepted or canceled. Current and former employees told the Journal that compliance workers escalated concerns about the surge in fraudulent deposits to Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan. According to people cited by the newspaper, Coplan responded: "Just keep growing and pay a fine if regulators ever find out." Polymarket has not publicly confirmed that the remark was made, and the company told the Journal that it maintains procedures to identify and respond to suspicious activity and remains committed to cooperating with regulators and law enforcement. Debit-Card Limits, Riskified Deployment Said to Lower Fraud Rates by May The Journal reported that elevated fraud continued for several months after February, though rejection rates did not return to the peak recorded during the first wave. By May, fraud rates had reportedly moved back toward normal industry levels after Polymarket limited how many debit cards users could connect to their accounts and brought in Riskified as an outside antifraud provider. An earlier report from The Information had separately described prediction-market operators, including Polymarket, strengthening card-fraud controls after criminals used stolen payment credentials and fake identities to create accounts. Visa reportedly pushed payment processors to tighten screening as disputed transactions increased. Riskified provides automated fraud-decision systems used to identify suspicious card activity before merchants approve transactions. Public material from the company describes its service as combining machine-learning risk scoring with merchant transaction controls, but Riskified has not publicly disclosed Polymarket-specific fraud numbers. The Journal further reported that Polymarket initially required some withdrawals to return to the same payment source that had funded an account, and that the platform later loosened that restriction, citing employees who raised concerns about financial-crime risks. Polymarket US Operates Under CFTC-Regulated QCX; Prior Penalty Cited QCX LLC, doing business as Polymarket US, is listed as a designated contract market and received its designation in July 2025, according to the CFTC. Polymarket US is legally separate from the company's international blockchain-based prediction market, which uses separate infrastructure and access rules, according to the report. The regulatory status differs from Polymarket's position in 2022, when the CFTC ordered the company to pay a $1.4 million civil penalty for offering event-based binary options without operating through a registered market. The settlement required Polymarket to wind down noncompliant markets and cease the violations cited in the order, according to the agency. The Journal reported that the CFTC is now investigating issues connected with Polymarket and that employees were instructed to preserve documents involving the February fraud incident and other matters; no new public CFTC enforcement release specifically addressing the February stolen-card episode was located as of Sept. 20. The reported investigation should be treated as an ongoing inquiry described by the Journal, not a finding that Polymarket violated federal law. Separate congressional scrutiny was already underway. On May 22, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform requested records from Polymarket concerning identity verification, suspicious activity, geographic restrictions and referrals to U.S. authorities. That inquiry centered on insider trading and sensitive information, not the stolen-card scheme reported by the Journal. Company Cites Strengthened Controls and Hires; Separate 2026 Incidents Reported Since the February incident, Polymarket has expanded its internal investigation and management functions. Shana Bautista, a former FBI investigator, joined as global head of investigations and intelligence, and the company named Warren Jenson, a former Amazon, Electronic Arts, Delta Air Lines and Nielsen finance executive, as its first chief financial officer on Sept. 10, the company said. Polymarket did not announce an IPO timetable when it appointed him, although the Journal reported that the company is preparing itself for a potential public listing. Polymarket's own market-integrity page says the company has referred more than 90 accounts to law enforcement and supplied authorities with details involving more than 315 wallets. The figures are company-reported and do not relate exclusively to payment-card fraud. The Journal reported separate account-security episodes in 2026. In June, Polymarket confirmed that a compromised third-party vendor injected malicious code into its frontend for some users; the company said it removed the affected dependency, contained the incident and would reimburse affected customers. Blockchain investigators later estimated losses at roughly $3.1 million across 11 wallets, according to the report. The Journal also reported a July incident involving nearly 500 users in which attackers used stolen personal information to access existing accounts and linked payment methods through an engineering weakness; Polymarket reportedly agreed to cover affected losses. The company's current position is that its fraud controls have been strengthened and that it works with law enforcement on suspicious activity. The Journal's report says February's payment-fraud rate had returned to industry norms by May after debit-card restrictions and the Riskified deployment. Independent outlets have emphasized that platform transparency and verified user identity remain unresolved questions for prediction markets as a category. Conclusion The company's response has included tighter limits on linked debit cards, an outside antifraud vendor, senior hires in investigations and finance, and stated cooperation with law enforcement and regulators. Whether those measures fully resolve the underlying risks remains an open question as of late September 2026. The dispute also illustrates a recurring pattern documented across financial markets – suspicious trading activity raising insider-trading concerns, as seen in the roughly $7 billion in oil futures trades flagged in March and April [3] and the $125 million oil trade reported ahead of a U.S.-Iran announcement [4]. Those episodes, like the Polymarket matter, remain under investigation, with no public conclusions as of this report. References NaturalNews.com. Polymarket is not a public stock. It is a private company seeking roughly $1 billion at a valuation near $21 billion and reportedly targeting an IPO within the next year. The current round includes roughly $300 million from 1789 Capital, the fund tied to Donald Trump Jr., and Intercontinental ExchangeICE-- — the parent of the New York Stock Exchange — invested $600 million in March. For an ordinary investor, that raises the stakes of the story in one specific way: the only route to touching this business is either a future IPO or a diversified exchange holding like ICE, and the compliance gap the Journal documented is the kind of thing that delays an IPO or caps the price paid at it.

The fraud alone is not the investment case against the business; attempted-theft losses that got stopped, and that Polymarket fixed by May, are a resolvable problem. The material question is what the episode says about the culture a public-company balance sheet would inherit. A venue that trades as a regulated U.S. platform but reacted to its first genuine stress test with "pay a fine if regulators ever find out" is carrying a cost no growth chart prices.

The break condition is simple to state. If the CFTC, IRS, and Justice Department reviews conclude the response was inadequate, or the IPO slips while JPMorganJPM-- stays on the sidelines, then the $21 billion valuation — which assumes a durable, licensed, investable franchise — reprices toward the risk. If the receipts show Polymarket's fixes held and the reviews clear it, the episode reads as the rough adolescence of a young regulated business, and the near miss stays a footnote. Which version is true is not something any retail investor can resolve by reading this article; it is something the disclosures, not the denials, will settle.

data.title: Polymarket Bug Reportedly Let Identity Thieves Into Existing Accounts
data.ai_summary: Nearly 500 Polymarket US accounts were compromised in late July via a password-free exploit, allowing thieves to access linked bank accounts and debit cards. The company said it would cover lost funds, but users reported thousands in losses and weeks of silence. A separate incident drained about $3.1 million in PUSD from a third-party vendor.
data.author: Kyle Torpey

industries.name: Fraud Detection, Scam Prevention & Account Takeover (Crypto)

data.full_text:
Nearly 500 Polymarket US users were hit in late July by a fraud attack that did not require a password, a username, or a compromised phone, according to a Wall Street Journal report published Saturday. A person who tried to create a new account with an existing trader’s personal information, such as a stolen Social Security number, was reportedly dropped into that trader’s live profile. Linked bank accounts and debit cards also became accessible, the report says.

With the seemingly constant drumbeat of new data breaches taking place these days, the ability to access someone else’s account by effectively using personal data as a password is an incredible security vulnerability. Just a few weeks ago, 153 million driver’s licenses were put on sale following the breach of an identity verification company.

The Journal, citing a person familiar with the matter, described the episode as an engineering problem and indicated the total amount stolen via the exploit was small. However, users told a different story in interviews with the media outlet. They described losses in the thousands of dollars and weeks of unanswered support messages.

One Polymarket user in the U.S. told the Journal he joined the prediction market platform to bet on the World Cup. In July, he logged in to find his positions sold and $5,783.51 in gains sent to a debit card he did not own. Polymarket credited his account $25 and offered no explanation. The user said he filed reports with local police, the FBI, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). “Polymarket US was silent for weeks and weeks,” he said. Support later put his account on hold after he submitted verification information twice but still did not address the missing funds.

A Polymarket spokeswoman told the Journal the company would cover lost money from the incident. The company has not published a public postmortem on the signup flaw.

Growth at Any Cost

The July attack sits inside a broader picture the Journal painted of a company that treated fraud acceptance as a cost of scaling. In February, payment processor Checkout.com warned Polymarket that thieves were tying stolen debit cards to thousands of new U.S. accounts, funding wagers, and trying to pull the money onto clean cards or accounts they controlled. Attempted theft ran to at least $10 million. At one point Checkout.com rejected more than 80% of the deposits it was handling as fraudulent, against an industry benchmark of roughly 1%.

Employees took the problem to CEO Shayne Coplan, but the compliance team’s recollection of his answer was that Coplan said to keep growing and pay a fine if regulators ever find out.

Fraud rates stayed elevated for months after February. By May, the Journal said, they had returned to industry norms after Polymarket limited debit cards per account and brought on antifraud contractor Riskified. Some customers were reimbursed while others clawed money back through their banks.

Polymarket and Kalshi’s Many Controversies

The July identity flaw was not Polymarket’s only security problem this year. In June the company said a compromised third-party vendor had injected a malicious script into its website frontend for some users. Blockchain monitors put the resulting drain of funds from the hack at about $3.1 million in PUSD, Polymarket’s dollar token, across at least 11 wallets. Polymarket said it removed the dependency and would refund affected users in full. Head of experience William LeGate wrote on X that there were “no user ‘losses’” because of those refunds.

Polymarket Under Attack Polymarket users were drained of ~$3.1M in PUSD on Polygon via phishing / malicious EIP-7702 delegated execution. Funds were converted to USDC.e via Relay, bridged to Ethereum, swapped to ETH, and consolidated at… pic.twitter.com/bG3GYZZ1D9 — AMLBot (@AMLBotHQ) June 27, 2026

That incident landed in the same week as a separate Wall Street Journal report that Polymarket had paid social media creators to film fake winning trades on replica versions of its site.

Insider trading has also been a seemingly non-stop issue with prediction market platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi. In May, a Google engineer was charged over a run of Polymarket wagers on Google’s most-searched people that prosecutors say relied on internal search data. Campaign staffers have described using unreleased internal polls to trade before the numbers hit the public. Even George Santos is accused of betting against his own appearance at the State of the Union after posting that he would attend, a case Kalshi referred to federal authorities. Of course, the most troubling cases involve military operations in Venezuela and Iran.

Both Polymarket and Kalshi ban insider trading on paper and have implemented policies to guard against this kind of activity. Additionally, Polymarket has tightened the screws on VPN-based users as bans and blocks piled up in more than 30 jurisdictions, including Spain, Indonesia, France, and the United Kingdom.

There’s also the fight with states that say sports contracts on prediction markets are just unlicensed sportsbooks. There were at least 20 ongoing cases related to this as of February of this year, and 38 states joined an amicus brief backing Maryland against Kalshi. Utah Gov. Spencer Cox called the products “gambling, pure and simple,” while the CFTC told states to get out of the way.

Prediction Markets Keep Getting Bigger Anyway

Of course, none of this has slowed down the industry’s growth. Combined monthly volume on Kalshi and both Polymarket venues rose from under $2 billion in August of last year to a peak of about $50.6 billion in July, according to The Block. August then slipped 15% to $45.3 billion, the first monthly decline in a year after the World Cup bump faded. During the World Cup, Kalshi alone printed $1 billion to $1.25 billion in sports volume on some days. This success enjoyed by these platforms has also led traditional sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel to get involved.

$15m to help get a generation of kids hooked on gambling is a choice. LeShame. https://t.co/g8IMDuSvOi — Haralabos Voulgaris (@haralabob) September 17, 2026

Indeed, sports contracts have been a key driver of growth for the prediction markets industry, which has led to criticism that this is really just degenerate gambling by another name. Former Dallas Mavericks analytics director and legendary NBA bettor Haralabos Voulgaris summarized this point of view in his response to the news regarding LeBron James’s new deal with Polymarket. “$15m to help get a generation of kids hooked on gambling is a choice,” Voulgaris wrote on X, and added “LeShame.”

James will reportedly be paid $15 million a year to endorse Polymarket, more than three times the amount the Philadelphia 76ers are paying him to play basketball this season.

However, prediction market proponents contend that the data on the probabilities of future events provides a separate benefit to society in the form of better signals regarding whether those events will occur. Indeed, a Federal Reserve staff paper on Kalshi’s contracts from earlier this year found that its federal funds and CPI markets offered statistically significant improvements over fed funds futures and professional forecasters.

The CFTC’s investigation, opened after the February attack, has already ordered employees to preserve internal records. That number is the story. "Fraud attack tests blockchain brand" is how this gets framed, but the blockchain never failed. Polymarket's pitch is that it runs on rails strangers can audit: positions settle in USDC on the Polygon network, and every trade is a public smart-contract event anyone can re-verify. The ledger was the one thing that behaved.

Ask Aime: How can you protect your investments from debit card fraud on trading platforms?

So the fraud attack didn't test whether the chain can be trusted. It tested whether the parts of Polymarket that are least like a blockchain can be trusted, and the answer it produced was worth reading as a business signal, not a forensics footnote.

Quick Backtesting Tool Symbol SPY Strategy Bollinger Bands Backtest Range Past 5 years

When "transparency" and "trust" are different things

Separate the two and the rest of the story lines up. A blockchain offers transparency: you can see where money moves. It does not offer trust, in the sense of an operator who is careful with your money. Transparency tells you an event happened; it tells you nothing about whether the people watching that event raced to grow before they raced to protect.

Polymarket's leadership picked that order, and the record is specific. Current and former employees told the WSJ that compliance staff raised the February fraud directly with CEO Shayne Coplan. His instruction, as reported, was to keep expanding and to pay any regulatory fines that surfaced rather than slow down. It took until May for fraud rates to return to normal, after Polymarket capped how many debit cards a user could connect and brought in an antifraud contractor, Riskified. And it did not end there: a separate July incident hit nearly 500 users through an engineering flaw that let attackers use stolen personal data to reach existing accounts, and Polymarket said it would make the victims whole.

Two readings, as always. The generous one: prodigious growth genuinely outpaced the controls, and the company says it has since added risk-management and compliance muscle. The honest one: this is a firm that, with its money where its mouth is, chose market share now and cleanup later. Both readings are compatible with the same facts, and the facts are what a valuation should be tested against — because a $21 billion company does not get to outrun discipline forever.

The numbers behind the $21 billion

The fraud report lands while Polymarket is sprinting toward a public listing. It is seeking $1 billion at roughly a $21 billion valuation, with Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital reportedly in for about $300 million; Intercontinental Exchange disclosed its prior $1.6 billion stake as a 22% position. In September it hired Warren Jenson, the ex-Amazon and ex-Delta CFO, as its first-ever finance chief — the classic pre-IPO move. Sacra estimates annualized revenue hit about $1 billion in June 2026, up from effectively zero in 2025, when the platform still charged no trading fees; today it earns mostly taker fees on volume, which is why growth and trust are the same line item. More volume of the wrong kind was not revenue worth keeping, because stolen-card volume came with chargebacks, reputational damage, and a paper trail for regulators.

That paper trail is already long. The CFTC has an open investigation; employees have been told to preserve records tied to the February attack and other matters; and Polymarket faces lawsuits over whether its markets are unlicensed gambling in some states. It is the same mix of tailwinds and liabilities that any young financial platform carries into its first public chapter — except most of them are not simultaneously telling investors "we chose growth, we'll pay the fine."

What an investor does with this before the IPO

You cannot buy Polymarket before it lists, so the honest move is not to trade it but to learn from it. Here is the checklist for any holding in this category, and it applies to the next trust-dependent crypto company you see, not just this one:

First, name the layer that actually holds customer money. If the pitch is "on-chain and trustless," ask whether the money enters and exits through a central keeper, a payment processor, and an identity check. Whatever the chain does, the rails decide how much can be stolen. Second, check whether the operator's growth incentives have ever lined up against custody hygiene — the fraud report and the 80% rejection rate are the evidence this writer would screen on. Third, treat "we'll pay the fine" as a stated operating principle, not a shrug. It is a real answer for a private company betting it can outgrow its fines; it is a different answer once the penalty lands on shareholders' earnings.

The mechanism here is simple, and it is the whole article: a ledger that cannot lie is not a platform whose incentives you should trust. The chain held in February, and that tells you nothing about whether the people running the platform wanted the growth more than they wanted the guardrails — they told you that themselves when they chose to keep scaling against a payment processor that was rejecting four of every five deposits.

This playbook expires the same way every growth-at-all-costs playbook does: when the fine or the acquisition grind arrives and is larger than the revenue the fog bought. Re-verify before the IPO lands by asking one question — did the company ever tell the story of February out loud, or did it wait for the WSJ to? Honest operators disclose the attack before they have to.

data.title: Polymarket hit by alleged $10M stolen-card fraud: Guest Post by crypto.news
data.ai_summary: Polymarket faced at least $10 million in attempted stolen-card fraud in February, with Checkout.com rejecting over 80% of deposits. Fraud rates returned to industry norms by May after card restrictions and Riskified were added. The CFTC is investigating, and Polymarket has expanded compliance and investigations.

industries.name: Crypto Payment Fraud, Chargeback & Risk Management

data.full_text:
Market Musing-g

Polymarket has come under renewed scrutiny after a Sept. 19 report said fraudsters used stolen debit cards on its U.S. platform in February to attempt at least $10 million in illicit withdrawals and wagers.

Summary Polymarket reportedly faced at least $10 million in attempted stolen-card fraud during February this year.

Checkout.com reportedly rejected more than 80% of Polymarket US deposits as fraudulent during February’s peak.

Polymarket says fraud rates later returned to industry norms after stronger card controls were introduced.

Polymarket US operates through QCX, a CFTC-designated contract market subject to federal derivatives oversight today.

Polymarket recently hired Warren Jenson as CFO while expanding compliance, investigations and risk management staffing.

The Wall Street Journal reported that criminals connected stolen cards to thousands of Polymarket US accounts, funded them and then tried to move the money through trading before withdrawing it to cards or accounts they controlled.

Polymarket reportedly saw fraud rejection rates top 80%

At the peak of the February attack, payment processor Checkout.com rejected more than 80% of deposits it handled for Polymarket as fraudulent, according to the Journal. The newspaper compared that rate with an industry level of roughly 1%.

The 80% figure has not been independently confirmed by Checkout.com in a public statement reviewed for this report. Checkout.com does provide merchants with fraud-scoring, transaction-filtering and authentication tools, while its current service terms state that merchants remain responsible for deciding whether transactions are accepted or canceled.

Current and former employees told the Journal that compliance workers escalated concerns about the surge to Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan. According to people cited by the newspaper, Coplan responded: “Just keep growing and pay a fine if regulators ever find out.”

Polymarket has not publicly confirmed that Coplan made the remark. The company told the Journal that it maintains procedures to identify and respond to suspicious activity and remains committed to cooperating with regulators and law enforcement.

The $10 million figure represents the amount fraudsters allegedly tried to move, not a confirmed loss suffered by customers or Polymarket. Public reporting reviewed for this article does not provide a final amount successfully withdrawn through the February scheme.

Card restrictions helped bring fraud rates down by May

The Journal reported that elevated fraud continued for several months after February, though rejection rates did not return to the peak recorded during the first wave. By May, fraud rates had reportedly moved back toward normal industry levels after Polymarket limited how many debit cards users could connect to their accounts and brought in Riskified as an outside antifraud provider.

An earlier report from The Information had separately described prediction-market operators, including Polymarket, strengthening card-fraud controls after criminals used stolen payment credentials and fake identities to create accounts. Visa reportedly pushed payment processors to tighten screening as disputed transactions increased.

Riskified provides automated fraud-decision systems used to identify suspicious card activity before merchants approve transactions. Public material from the company describes its service as combining machine-learning risk scoring with merchant transaction controls, but Riskified has not publicly disclosed Polymarket-specific fraud numbers.

The Journal further reported that Polymarket initially required some withdrawals to return to the same payment source that had funded an account. The platform later loosened that restriction, according to the report, which cited employees who raised concerns about financial-crime risks.

Polymarket’s current U.S. rulebook gives the exchange authority to restrict accounts, place customers into liquidation-only status and take other steps to protect customers and market integrity. The CFTC filing containing the March 20 version was certified in April.

Polymarket US operates under CFTC-regulated QCX

Polymarket US is legally separate from the company’s international blockchain-based prediction market.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s current register lists QCX LLC, doing business as Polymarket US, as a designated contract market. QCX received its designation in July 2025 before operating under the Polymarket US name.

As previously explained in Polymarket’s two-platform structure , U.S. customers trade through the federally regulated exchange, while the international product uses separate blockchain infrastructure and access rules.

The regulatory status differs from Polymarket’s position in 2022, when the CFTC ordered the company to pay a $1.4 million civil penalty for offering event-based binary options without operating through a registered market. The settlement required Polymarket to wind down noncompliant markets and cease the violations cited in the order.

The Journal reported that the CFTC is now investigating issues connected with Polymarket and that employees were instructed to preserve documents involving the February fraud incident and other matters.

No new public CFTC enforcement release specifically addressing the February stolen-card episode was located as of Sept. 20. The reported investigation should therefore be treated as an ongoing inquiry described by the Journal, not a finding that Polymarket violated federal law.

Separate congressional scrutiny was already underway. On May 22, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform requested records from Polymarket concerning identity verification, suspicious activity, geographic restrictions and referrals to U.S. authorities.

The committee specifically requested documents showing the number and disposition of suspicious-activity referrals since Jan. 1, 2024. That inquiry centered on insider trading and sensitive information, not the stolen-card scheme reported this weekend.

Polymarket has expanded investigations and finance teams

Since the February incident, Polymarket has built out its internal investigation and management functions. Shana Bautista, a former FBI investigator, joined as global head of investigations and intelligence. Reuters reported in August that the company uses blockchain analytics, machine learning and trading surveillance to identify anomalous behavior.

Polymarket’s own market-integrity page says the company has referred more than 90 accounts to law enforcement and supplied authorities with details involving more than 315 wallets. The figures are company-reported and do not relate exclusively to payment-card fraud.

Federal authorities have publicly acknowledged cooperation in at least one separate case. In April, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York said Polymarket cooperated with investigators in the case of an Army service member accused of using classified information to trade event contracts.

The CFTC filed a parallel insider-trading complaint alleging that the defendant earned more than $404,000 trading a market related to the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The case remains separate from the February payment-card allegations.

Polymarket added another senior executive on Sept. 10 when it named Warren Jenson its first chief financial officer. The CFO appointment , Jenson previously served in senior finance roles at Amazon, Electronic Arts, Delta Air Lines and Nielsen.

The company said Jenson will oversee finance, capital strategy and long-range planning. Polymarket did not announce an IPO timetable when it appointed him, although the Journal reported that the company is preparing itself for a potential public listing.

Polymarket has been raising large amounts of private capital in parallel. ICE, the parent of the New York Stock Exchange, disclosed a further $600 million cash investment in March after investing $1 billion in 2025.

As recent Polymarket funding coverage reported , the company has separately been seeking roughly $1 billion in new capital at a valuation near $21 billion. The financing has not been presented by Polymarket as a formal IPO filing.

Separate security incidents added pressure during 2026

Payment fraud has not been the company’s only security issue this year. In June, Polymarket confirmed that a compromised third-party vendor injected malicious code into its frontend for some users. The company said it removed the affected dependency, contained the incident and would reimburse affected customers.

The June event was technically separate from the February stolen-card activity. It involved compromised web infrastructure and wallet interactions, while the earlier scheme reportedly relied on stolen debit-card credentials and account funding.

The Journal reported another account-security episode in July involving nearly 500 users. According to its account, attackers used stolen personal information to access existing accounts and linked payment methods through an engineering weakness. Polymarket reportedly agreed to cover affected losses.

No public Polymarket notice reviewed for this report provides an independently confirmed loss total from that July incident.

The company’s current position is that its fraud controls have been strengthened and that it works with law enforcement on suspicious activity. The Journal’s report says February’s payment-fraud rate had returned to industry norms by May after debit-card restrictions and the Riskified deployment.
