data.title: Top International Chargeback Solutions for Cross-Border Ecommerce in 2026
data.ai_summary: The article reviews leading international chargeback solutions for cross-border ecommerce in 2026, highlighting platforms such as Chargeflow, Ethoca, and Verifi that help merchants manage disputes across multiple markets. It details how these tools utilize global card network alerts and automated evidence gathering to mitigate risks associated with unfamiliar fraud patterns and currency fluctuations. The piece also outlines key evaluation criteria for merchants, including data residency compliance and regional win-rates.
data.author: Khizar Nisar
data.full_text:
Selling across borders multiplies the chargeback problem in ways a single-market merchant rarely deals with: unfamiliar fraud patterns, different card network enforcement by region, and currency conversion disputes that domestic sellers never see. This roundup covers the international chargeback solutions cross-border ecommerce businesses are using in 2026 to keep disputes manageable across multiple markets at once.

Why cross-border chargebacks are a different problem than domestic ones

A merchant selling only within its home market builds up a fraud and dispute history that its tools, and its own instincts, can learn from over time. That history doesn’t transfer cleanly to a new market.

Currency fluctuations between the purchase date and the statement date generate their own category of disputes when a customer doesn’t recognize a slightly different charged amount. Shipping timelines are longer and less predictable across borders, which increases “item not received” disputes simply because customers wait longer and grow impatient sooner.

On top of that, Visa’s and Mastercard’s dispute-monitoring thresholds apply globally, but the practical risk tolerance and enforcement can vary by region and by the specific acquiring bank relationship in that market. A merchant expanding into three or four new countries at once can end up managing what amounts to three or four different risk profiles simultaneously, without three or four times the staff to handle it.

Best international chargeback solutions in 2026

1. Chargeflow

Chargeflow is built around a global operating model rather than a single-market one, supporting multi-store and multi-processor setups and reporting activity across 90 countries.

For a cross-border merchant, that breadth matters because the platform’s evidence-automation and prevention systems have been trained on dispute patterns across many markets rather than just one, which helps when a merchant is entering a country its own transaction history doesn’t cover yet.

On the prevention side, Chargeflow’s Alerts product connects to Visa and Mastercard’s dispute-alert networks, which operate consistently across markets even when local fraud behavior differs, catching a likely chargeback before it’s formally filed. The company reports Alerts can cut a merchant’s chargeback rate by up to 90% and begins working within 24 hours.

For disputes that do get filed, the platform automates evidence gathering and submission and reports a 100% submission rate, which matters across time zones and currencies where a manually tracked deadline is easy to miscalculate.

Pricing is success-based, meaning a merchant only pays when Chargeflow actually recovers a chargeback, with no long-term contract, which keeps costs proportional to actual dispute volume as a merchant scales into new markets rather than requiring a renegotiated flat fee each time.

The platform runs on SOC 2 Type 2 and GDPR-compliant infrastructure with data stored in US data centers, connects to more than 100 platforms including Shopify, Stripe, WooCommerce, and PayPal, and the company states it has recovered more than $200 million for merchants collectively.

Multi-store, multi-processor support built for cross-border operations

Prevention via Visa/Mastercard alert networks that work consistently across markets

Success-based pricing that scales cleanly as a merchant expands into new countries

2. Ethoca

Best for: merchants who want early visibility into Mastercard disputes across multiple markets.

Ethoca, run by Mastercard, connects merchants and issuing banks so a dispute can be resolved through a refund before it escalates into a formal chargeback, and it operates across Mastercard’s global network rather than being limited to specific regions.

Mastercard’s global merchant-issuer alert network

Refund-based resolution before formal chargebacks

Works consistently across the markets Mastercard operates in

3. Verifi

Best for: merchants who need the same early-warning coverage on Visa transactions internationally.

Verifi runs Visa’s Cardholder Dispute Resolution Network, alerting merchants to a likely dispute before it becomes a chargeback across Visa’s global footprint. Most cross-border merchants run Verifi and Ethoca together to cover both major networks internationally.

Real-time Visa dispute alerts across international markets

Refund window that avoids a formal chargeback being filed

Typically paired with Ethoca for full network coverage

4. ClearSale

Best for: merchants with significant order volume in Latin America or other markets where local review expertise helps.

ClearSale combines automated screening with a human review team, and its strongest coverage is in Latin American markets where local fraud patterns and documentation norms don’t always map cleanly onto a generic global model. That local expertise can matter more than raw model sophistication in specific regions.

Automated screening plus human manual review

Particularly strong Latin American market coverage

Useful where local fraud patterns differ from global norms

5. Riskified

Best for: merchants actively expanding into several new countries at once.

Riskified offers a chargeback guarantee on approved orders and draws on cross-merchant fraud data spanning many international markets, which helps most in the early stages of entering a country where the merchant’s own data is still thin.

Chargeback guarantee on approved international orders

Cross-merchant fraud intelligence across many markets

Strong fit during active multi-country expansion

6. Signifyd

Best for: merchants who want a financial guarantee alongside automated cross-border order decisions.

Signifyd reviews orders and backs its decisions with a guarantee against fraud-related chargebacks, which can offset some of the added uncertainty that comes with reviewing orders from markets a merchant is newer to.

Financial guarantee on approved orders

Automated order decisioning at checkout

Fee structure suited to higher international order volumes

7. Kount

Best for: merchants that need fraud prevention paired with identity verification across markets with different compliance rules.

Kount, an Equifax company, combines fraud detection with identity-verification tools, which helps merchants navigate the different know-your-customer and age-verification requirements that can vary significantly from one country to the next.

Fraud detection paired with identity verification

Backed by Equifax data and infrastructure

Useful where compliance requirements differ by market

8. Forter

Best for: merchants who want to minimize false declines on legitimate customers while expanding internationally.

Forter builds identity-trust profiles across its merchant network to make approve/decline decisions, with a stated focus on reducing false declines. That matters more in cross-border sales, where an unfamiliar billing address or device can look riskier to a generic model than it actually is for a legitimate customer.

Identity-based trust scoring shared across a global merchant network

Focus on reducing false declines for legitimate international customers

More common in larger, enterprise-scale cross-border implementations

9. Accertify

Best for: large merchants that want an enterprise-grade platform with deep regional configurability.

Accertify, owned by American Express, supports enterprise-level fraud and chargeback management with the configurability to tune rules differently by region, which suits a merchant with the internal resources to manage that complexity directly rather than relying on a vendor’s default global settings.

Deep, region-specific configurability

Backed by American Express infrastructure

Higher implementation effort, suited to larger cross-border operations

What cross-border merchants should check before choosing a provider

Data residency and compliance requirements should come first, before comparing features. Different markets have different rules about where transaction and cardholder data can be processed and stored, and that alone can rule out certain vendors before anything else gets evaluated.

From there, check whether a provider’s prevention model relies on network-level alerts tied to Visa and Mastercard, which behave consistently everywhere, or purely on its own proprietary fraud scoring built from its existing merchant base, since the second type tends to be less reliable in a market where neither the merchant nor the vendor has much transaction history yet.

Currency handling is a smaller but real detail worth checking too. A provider that clearly separates currency-conversion-related disputes from other reason codes in its reporting makes it much easier to spot when a specific market’s disputes are actually a currency-display problem on the checkout page rather than a fraud or fulfillment issue, which is a very different fix.

Language and local documentation norms matter more than most merchants expect going in.



A representment case built around US-style evidence conventions doesn’t always translate cleanly to how a dispute gets evaluated by an issuing bank in another region, and a provider with actual experience winning cases in a specific market tends to structure evidence differently for that market rather than submitting the same template everywhere.

That’s a harder thing to evaluate from a sales pitch alone, so asking a vendor directly about regional win-rate differences, not just a single blended number, is worth doing before committing.

Shipping and fulfillment partners add another wrinkle specific to cross-border sales. Longer transit times and customs delays both increase the odds of an “item not received” dispute simply because customers wait longer, and evidence requirements around proof of delivery can differ by destination country’s postal system.

A provider that automatically pulls tracking data at the carrier level, rather than requiring a merchant to manually attach it per case, saves real time once order volume across several countries starts adding up.

Frequently asked questions

Do chargeback rules differ significantly between countries?

The core Visa and Mastercard dispute frameworks apply globally, but practical enforcement, typical dispute reason codes, and risk tolerance can vary by region and by the specific acquiring bank relationship in that market.

Why do currency differences cause chargebacks?

A customer sometimes doesn’t recognize a charge on their statement if the converted amount differs from what they expected at checkout, due to exchange rate movement between the purchase and the statement date, which can lead them to dispute a legitimate transaction.

Should a cross-border merchant use multiple chargeback tools at once?

Many do, commonly pairing network-level alert services like Verifi and Ethoca with a broader platform that handles prevention and dispute automation together, since each layer addresses a different part of the problem across different markets.

How long does it typically take to see results after adding a prevention layer internationally?

Alert-based prevention tied to card networks can start flagging likely disputes within a day or two of setup, though a clear read on the overall impact to a merchant’s chargeback rate in a new market usually takes a month or two of data to assess properly.

New Travel Industry report reveals sophisticated fraud rings are exploiting trusted customer behaviors across flights, hotels, and travel platforms

NEW YORK --(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Riskified (NYSE: RSKD), a global leader in ecommerce fraud and risk intelligence, today released new findings from its Travel Industry Insights report, revealing how sophisticated fraud rings and AI-enabled fraudsters are evolving their tactics across airlines, hotels, and online travel platforms. Riskified’s analysis shows that fraudsters are increasingly adapting their behavior to resemble legitimate travelers, making traditional fraud indicators less reliable and creating new challenges for travel merchants.

Riskified’s analysis of hundreds of millions of travel transactions across flights, hotels, and land transportation found that flight fraud risk increased through the first five months of 2026, with May 2026 marking the sharpest year-over-year increase at 32% compared to May 2025. The findings show that sophisticated fraud activity is not limited to predictable travel peaks, with organized fraud rings continuously adjusting their methods throughout the year.

Riskified's travel network includes more than 60 travel merchants and has processed $828 billion in cumulative travel transactions across flights, hotels, and land transportation as of June 2026. This extensive visibility highlights how fraudsters are challenging long-standing assumptions about what legitimate travel behavior looks like.

Presented in Riskified’s latest Risk Rundown, “Booking scams are taking off,” the data reveals several key shifts in travel fraud patterns:

Traditional identity signals are changing: While billing-name-to-passenger-name mismatches remained 2.5x riskier in 2025, flight transactions where the billing name matched the passenger name saw a significant increase in risk since November 2025, reaching more than 30% above the January 2025 baseline.

While billing-name-to-passenger-name mismatches remained 2.5x riskier in 2025, flight transactions where the billing name matched the passenger name saw a significant increase in risk since November 2025, reaching more than above the January 2025 baseline. Last-minute bookings remain a major challenge: Flight purchases made less than seven days before departure were 2.3x riskier than other bookings, creating a challenge for merchants balancing fast customer experiences with fraud prevention.

Fraudsters are targeting valuable travel accounts: Loyalty programs, rewards points, and stored customer information remain attractive targets, with fraudsters monetizing compromised accounts by selling points for cash, redeeming them for gift cards, or using them to fund fraudulent bookings.

Loyalty programs, rewards points, and stored customer information remain attractive targets, with fraudsters monetizing compromised accounts by selling points for cash, redeeming them for gift cards, or using them to fund fraudulent bookings. Sophisticated fraud extends beyond the transaction: Fraudsters are using compromised identities, devices, and accounts to execute high-value purchases across travel and related industries.

“Each year, we analyze fraud trends across the travel industry, and it’s striking to see how quickly attack vectors evolve as fraudsters adapt to the signals merchants use to identify risk,” said Jeff Otto, CMO at Riskified. “A behavior that may have historically indicated a trusted customer can become a target for exploitation once fraud rings learn how to replicate it. Travel businesses need intelligence that continuously adapts to changing fraud patterns while helping them deliver seamless experiences for legitimate travelers.”

The analysis also highlights unique challenges across other travel categories. In hotels, July and August generated the highest revenue but also carried the highest potential fraud-loss exposure. Fraud activity can increase unexpectedly, with April 2025 identified as the riskiest month, 20% above the yearly average. Luxury properties were particularly targeted, with five-star hotels representing the riskiest segment overall.

Riskified also observed increased abuse of both consumer and travel provider accounts on travel platforms, where fraudsters use phishing, breaches, or other methods to compromise verified accounts. These stolen identities can provide access to guest communications, reservation details, and trusted platform relationships, making fraudulent activity more difficult to detect.

As travel continues to expand globally, merchants face increasing pressure to maximize conversion while managing increasingly sophisticated fraud. Riskified’s travel intelligence combines network-level insights, customer behavior analysis, and transaction data to help travel businesses make more accurate decisions throughout the customer journey.

Learn more about Riskified’s Travel industry expertise at Riskified.com.

Report Methodology

The findings in “Riskified Travel Industry Insights: Flights, Hotels & Land Transportation” are based on Riskified’s analysis of travel transaction data from a sample of travel merchants across its global merchant network, including airlines, online travel agencies, hotels, and land transportation providers. The analysis includes full-year 2025 data and 2026 year-to-date trends.

data.title: 11 Companies That Help Employees Grow Their Careers
data.ai_summary: The article profiles eleven employees from various companies, including Riot Platforms, Bevi, and Riskified, detailing their career growth and internal mobility experiences. It highlights how these organizations foster professional development through supportive cultures, expanded responsibilities, and opportunities for strategic impact. The narrative emphasizes that employee retention is significantly influenced by the availability of resources and support for advancing one's career.
data.full_text:
People join companies for all sorts of reasons — competitive pay, benefits, a flexible schedule — but there’s one factor that plays a significant role in whether they will stay: career growth opportunities.

Just ask Hunter Martin, a manager of software engineering at Riot Platforms, Inc., which operates large-scale data centers and bitcoin mining networks. He joined the company out of a desire to own systems end to end, and so far, that’s exactly what he’s been able to do.

“What started as ownership of individual applications became ownership of how software gets built here,” Martin said.

It’s a similar story for Territory Sales Manager Trevor Webb, who joined connected beverage platform provider Bevi because he wanted to join a company where he could make an immediate impact. Over the past two and a half years, he has taken on several different roles and responsibilities, encouraged by others who believed in his abilities.

“Rather than feeling like I had to wait years for new opportunities, I was encouraged to raise my hand for new challenges and prove what I was capable of,” Webb said. “That culture of trust and internal mobility has made all the difference.”

For these two professionals and nine others, having resources and support to grow has been a career game-changer. Read on to learn more about how their employers have helped them achieve their professional goals.

Riot Platforms, Inc. operates large-scale data centers and bitcoin mining networks across the United States.

What originally attracted you to Riot Platforms, Inc., and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

The pace. Riot moves fast, and I wanted a role where I could genuinely own systems end to end rather than contribute pieces of someone else’s. That’s what brought me in, and it’s the same thing that’s kept me here; the scope has just kept expanding. What started as ownership of individual applications became ownership of how software gets built here.

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Riot Platforms, Inc.?

I started as a software engineer and have since moved into managing software engineering for Riot. The biggest change wasn’t the title; it was the shape of the accountability. I’m now responsible for the entire software development function: the team, the standards we hold ourselves to and the direction we take. Learning to be accountable for outcomes I don’t personally produce has been the steepest and most valuable part of that growth.

“Learning to be accountable for outcomes I don’t personally produce has been the steepest and most valuable part of that growth.”

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

Stepping into the software engineering manager role. Up to that point, my value was measured by what I shipped. Almost overnight, it became about setting strategy, deciding what the team builds, how we build it and why. The first time I found myself defining direction for a system I wasn’t going to write a single line of code for and trusting the team to execute, it was obvious how far I’d come from where I started.

Amalgamated Sugar produces sugar from sugar beets.

What originally attracted you to Amalgamated Sugar, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I was originally attracted to the company because of its reputation. What’s kept me here is the combination of the people and the opportunities. I’ve really appreciated working with a supportive team and leadership that encourages growth. Over time, I’ve been able to take on new responsibilities, build my skills and see the impact of my work. That sense of progress and being part of something meaningful has made me want to stay and continue growing with the company.

“Over time, I’ve been able to take on new responsibilities, build my skills and see the impact of my work.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Amalgamated Sugar?

During my time here, I’ve grown both professionally and personally. When I first started, I focused on learning the core responsibilities of my role and understanding how the team operates. Over time, I’ve been able to take on additional responsibilities, improve my organizational and problem-solving skills, and become more confident in handling day-to-day challenges independently

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

One experience that really made me feel proud to work here was being part of organizing and setting up our annual meeting for the executive team, board members and growers. It’s such an important event, and having the opportunity to contribute behind the scenes to make sure everything runs smoothly was really rewarding.

I especially valued working closely with the other admins. We collaborated on coordinating logistics, managing details and supporting one another to ensure everything came together successfully. It was exciting to be part of a team effort that brings so many key people together. Seeing the event come together and knowing I played a role in that made me feel proud of my work and the team I’m part of.

Trevor Webb Territory Sales Manager • Bevi

Best known for its Smart Water Coolers®, Bevi has grown into the leading connected beverage platform, combining hardware, data and beverage innovation to deliver premium still, sparkling, flavored and enhanced drinks on demand.

What originally attracted you to Bevi, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

What first attracted me to Bevi was the opportunity to join a fast-growing company where I could make an immediate impact. The product was innovative, the mission made sense, and during the interview process it was clear that the people genuinely cared about helping one another succeed.

What has kept me here for the last two and a half years is the opportunity to continuously grow. Since joining, I’ve had the chance to take on several new roles and responsibilities, and each transition has come with incredible support from managers and teammates who trusted me to step outside my comfort zone. Rather than feeling like I had to wait years for new opportunities, I was encouraged to raise my hand for new challenges and prove what I was capable of. That culture of trust and internal mobility has made all the difference. It’s rewarding to work somewhere that invests in its employees and creates opportunities to build meaningful careers instead of having to look elsewhere for the next step.

“Since joining, I’ve had the chance to take on several new roles and responsibilities, and each transition has come with incredible support from managers and teammates who trusted me to step outside my comfort zone.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Bevi?

I’ve grown in almost every aspect of my career. I joined Bevi as an enterprise business development representative, where I built the fundamentals of prospecting, relationship-building and creating new opportunities. Since then, I’ve had the opportunity to support multiple teams and territories, contribute to our expansion into the United Kingdom and Ireland, and most recently, become the territory manager for the Northeast. Each role has required a different skill set. I’ve gone from generating pipeline to managing customer relationships, partnering with distributors, working with enterprise accounts and helping drive growth across an entire region. Along the way, I’ve become much more confident communicating with executive stakeholders, solving problems collaboratively and adapting quickly to new challenges.

One thing I appreciate most is that my growth wasn’t limited to formal promotions. My managers consistently gave me opportunities to stretch beyond my current role, whether that meant taking ownership of new projects, supporting different territories or stepping in wherever the business needed me. Those experiences accelerated my development and prepared me for the role I’m in today.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

One experience that really stands out was having the opportunity to help support Bevi’s expansion into the United Kingdom and Ireland. Being part of a project of that magnitude is something I’ll never forget, and knowing I played a role in helping establish our early success in a new market was incredibly rewarding. More recently, I’ve had the opportunity to step into different roles as the business has evolved and take on new challenges whenever they arise. Being trusted with those opportunities has been both humbling and motivating, and it reminded me of the impact I am making as well as the confidence my leaders had in me. Looking back, those experiences made me realize just how much I’ve grown since my first day at Bevi. I wasn’t just executing my own responsibilities anymore; I was thinking strategically, collaborating across teams and helping partners and customers find long-term solutions. When I was ultimately promoted to Territory Manager for the Northeast, it felt like a reflection of all those experiences and the trust the company had placed in me along the way. It’s been incredibly rewarding to see how much I’ve developed, and I’m excited to continue growing.

Jack Niesz Super Enterprise Business Development • Riskified

Riskified’s AI-powered fraud and risk intelligence platform analyzes the individual behind each interaction to provide real-time decisions and robust identity-based insights.

What originally attracted you to Riskified, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I wanted to join a company with an established, strong sales team so I could be a sponge in my first few months. Riskified had that, and it was already respected for how it helps retailers prevent fraud. That combination is what originally attracted me to the company. It was obvious during my interview process that Riskified had exactly what I was looking for.

What’s kept me here is the people I work with and the constant support I receive from everyone in the sales organization. I’ve always felt accounted for, and my peers are super welcoming and eager to lend a helping hand. It’s been rewarding to go from being the person who asks all the questions to being someone new hires now come to for direction.

“What’s kept me here is the people I work with and the constant support I receive from everyone in the sales organization.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Riskified?

It’s hard to put into words how much I’ve developed professionally over the past year and a half at Riskified. Flying out to different cities across the country to sit down with e-commerce leaders face to face is both challenging and exciting. Meeting with executives at well-known companies can be intimidating at first, but confidence in our product and myself turns any anxiety into curiosity and excitement to find out how we can help them tackle fraud or abuse. I’ve developed far more here than I thought possible when I started in May 2025.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

The Shoptalk Conference in Las Vegas this past March was a turning point that made me realize I was well on my way. Our booth sat in a prime foot-traffic location, and the booth behind us had puppies, which helped, of course. The in-depth conversations I had there were where I noticed how much I’d learned. My colleagues and I had several productive conversations with merchants facing a range of situations, many of whom have turned into real partnerships.

Live conversations and experiences with people build trust in a way that an email or a phone call never can. They’re where you learn what a retailer is actually up against, and that understanding is what turns into partnerships that last. I think everyone on the business development team here will tell you that conferences and other face-to-face events are where a lot of that groundwork gets done.

Natasha Raikar Chief of Staff, People • FareHarbor

FareHarbor creates tools for tour and activity operators, like boat rentals, food tours, outdoor experiences, events and more.

What originally attracted you to FareHarbor, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I joined FareHarbor more than seven years ago because of the people, the energy and the opportunity to work in an industry that helps create unforgettable experiences. What has kept me here is that the company has never stood still. I’ve watched FareHarbor adapt through rapid growth, industry shifts, a global pandemic and continued innovation. Every challenge created new opportunities to learn, contribute and grow alongside the business.

One thing I’ve learned is that growth here isn’t tied to a title; it’s tied to how you show up. If you’re curious, willing to step outside your comfort zone and embrace new challenges, people notice. Leaders invest in you, trust you with meaningful work and encourage you to explore new paths. My career has evolved because FareHarbor kept evolving, and I was fortunate to grow right alongside it.

“If you’re curious, willing to step outside your comfort zone and embrace new challenges, people notice.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at FareHarbor?

When I joined FareHarbor as a business development associate, I was new to both the travel and tech industries. I had a lot to learn, but a strong onboarding experience and a manager who encouraged me to stretch beyond my role gave me the confidence to dive in. Whether facilitating internal training, taking on special projects or jumping in wherever help was needed during the pandemic, every opportunity expanded my understanding of our product, our business and the industry.

Over time, I realized what energized me most was helping people grow, so I pursued a position on the people team. As a learning and development specialist, I embraced opportunities to keep learning myself. I took advantage of our learning platforms, shadowed leaders across FareHarbor and Booking.com, and sought mentorship from our chief of staff to the CEO. Through her guidance, and by seeking out increasingly strategic work, I developed skills in project management, stakeholder partnership and strategic planning that ultimately led me to my current role as chief of staff for the people team.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

There have been several moments, but two projects stand out.

The first was taking ownership of our Work Abroad Program. What started as an idea on paper became a companywide program that I built and led during its first two years. It required navigating operational complexities while partnering with leaders across FareHarbor to strengthen connections across our global offices. Seeing the program come to life and help employees grow professionally has been incredibly rewarding.

The second was leading the development of our Leadership Anchors. It wasn’t just another project; it helped define how we expect our leaders to navigate change, develop their teams, collaborate and deliver results. Collaborating with senior leaders to shape something that will influence the company for years to come strengthened my stakeholder management, strategic thinking and execution skills.

Neither opportunity came with a playbook. Leaders empowered me to turn ideas into reality, giving me the confidence to tackle other challenges that ultimately led me to my current role. Today, I’m excited to serve as a mentor in our mentorship program and support others in their career growth.

Playground’s child care management software is designed to help child care programs streamline their operations and administration.

What originally attracted you to Fortin, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I honestly didn’t know much about the child care industry before joining Playground, but I was immediately drawn to how fast-paced the company is. The product is constantly evolving, which keeps things interesting for both our customers and our team. Every day brings something new, so you’re always learning, adapting and picking up new skills.

Beyond the fast pace, the company culture and mentality has been a huge reason I’ve stayed. If you have a great idea, you’re encouraged to take ownership of it and see it through from start to finish. That’s not something you find everywhere. It’s incredibly rewarding to see your work have a direct impact on both the company and the customers we serve.

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Playground?

One of the biggest ways I’ve grown is by learning to balance a wide variety of responsibilities, many of which extend beyond my official role. At Playground, you’re not put into a box. If you’re willing to take initiative, dedicate yourself to something and prove yourself, the company recognizes that and gives you opportunities to grow.

“If you’re willing to take initiative, dedicate yourself to something and prove yourself, the company recognizes that and gives you opportunities to grow.”

I genuinely feel like I’ve learned more in the past year at Playground than I would have in several years at many other companies. A big part of that is because Playground has embraced my interests and given me opportunities to develop them, which has accelerated both my professional growth and my confidence.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

One moment that really stood out was being asked to help train our first official new-hire cohort. I had the opportunity to travel to Denver to meet the new team members and lead product training, which was an incredibly rewarding experience.

It meant a lot to know that Playground trusted me to teach others about our product and represent the company in that way. Having both my managers and peers show that level of confidence in my product knowledge, especially this early in my career, was a huge milestone and really made me realize how much I had grown in my role.

Domino Data Lab’s enterprise machine learning operations platform is designed to accelerate the development and deployment of data science work, helping organizations develop better medicines, grow more productive crops and more.

What originally attracted you to Domino Data Lab, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I was drawn to Domino by the prospect of tackling complex challenges for our public-sector clients and exploring how AI/ML could accelerate mission-critical use cases. I wanted to dive deeper into the field and be at the forefront of industry innovation. What has kept me here, however, is the culture. Working alongside such a deeply motivated team is incredibly inspiring. No matter their role or how busy their schedules are, people here are always willing to lend a hand and support one another’s growth.

“No matter their role or how busy their schedules are, people here are always willing to lend a hand and support one another’s growth.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Domino Data Lab?

My time at Domino has transformed how I approach AI/ML, shifting my lens from a purely technical standpoint to a broader business and strategic one. The startup environment naturally demands a high degree of responsibility and autonomy. Having the freedom to truly own my work has allowed me to mature as both an individual contributor and a leader. Furthermore, collaborating with diverse clients at varying stages of their AI journeys has shaped my perspective, allowing me to approach high-level conversations strategically and design use cases that genuinely excite our partners.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

My growth at Domino has been multifaceted, so it’s hard to share just one. My realization of technical growth came when I had the privilege of speaking at the Geospatial Intelligence Foundation’s 2026 conference on Autonomous Geospatial Knowledge Graphs. Presenting complex technical content that defense leaders could take back to optimize their organizations was an incredible milestone, and it cemented my place as a thought leader in the field. My realization of growth from a functional standpoint came when I was tapped to lead our forward deployed engineering arm. It was a validation of my ability to translate complex business problems into exciting technical solutions. This role has taken me to various customer offices to sit down with executive leadership and listen to how they view AI in the context of broader global impact. Being in those rooms, advising top-tier leaders, is a clear reflection of how much I’ve grown since day one.

Golden Hippo builds and operates health and wellness brands for both humans and their pets.

What originally attracted you to Golden Hippo, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I applied for a video editor position through Craigslist back in 2016. Honestly, I was just looking for an editing job with good benefits. My English wasn’t very strong at the time since it’s my second language. I think the fact that my main focus has always been telling stories through visuals actually worked in my favor.

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Golden Hippo?

I’ve never really been interested in titles. I’ve always been interested in the blank spaces and the opportunities. Every role I’ve had here started as a blank space. There wasn’t a creative director. There wasn’t a VP of creative. As the company grew, I kept seeing opportunities where creativity could make a bigger impact.

“As the company grew, I kept seeing opportunities where creativity could make a bigger impact.”

Instead of asking, “Whose job is this?” I usually found myself thinking, “Someone has to build this if we want to keep growing.”

So I’d raise my hand, figure it out, and build it alongside the incredible team at Ad Creative Team. Looking back, that’s probably been the biggest theme of my career.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

The best part hasn’t been my own growth. It’s been watching the people around me win! (Launching winning ads, earning “Win of the Year,” leading celebrity shoots and editing amazing Video Sales Letters).

At the end of the day, winning ads come and go. What lasts are the people behind them. Great people continue to raise the bar long after the ads are gone.

If my career has taught me anything, it’s that some of the best opportunities aren’t the ones you’re given — they’re the ones you create.

Allie Zell Strategy Director • Terakeet

Terakeet is an owned asset optimization partner for Fortune 500 companies dedicated to helping brands reach consumers as they search for solutions.

What originally attracted you to Terakeet, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

After graduating from college with a leadership and management degree, I wasn’t exactly sure what I wanted to do or what industry I wanted to work in. Terakeet was one of the only local Syracuse companies offering a fun and inviting work environment. I knew a few people who already worked there, and they spoke highly of the work and mission they were on. I guess you can say the rest is history. Twelve years later, I’m proud to say that I’ve worked in multiple departments, grown my career, helped create processes, supported multiple company shifts and won the company Chili Cook-Off two years in a row. In all seriousness, an important piece of what has kept me at Terakeet is the people. We spend one-third of our lives at work, so the people you work with matter. It’s pretty special to be able to work with people you consider your friends.

“It’s pretty special to be able to work with people you consider your friends.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Terakeet?

Everything about me has grown and developed because of my time at Terakeet. I became an adult at Terakeet, so my time here is truly an important piece of who I am today. I learned how to be a professional. I learned how to communicate with people, especially executives and Fortune 500 leaders. I learned how hard work can turn into advancement. I learned how crucial teamwork is. I learned how important work-life balance is.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

There are a few projects that come to mind, but honestly, what makes me beam with pride most is being described as the “the best of the best” to a client by my co-workers. It has made me realize how much I’ve grown in my role as a strategy director, and that the people I work with think this highly of me and my work.

Established in 2021, firsthand Health Inc supports individuals living with serious mental and physical illnesses by helping them connect with peer support, social benefits and community resources, and care providers.

What originally attracted you to firsthand Health, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

What originally attracted me to firsthand was its mission and its commitment to helping individuals live their best possible lives. I was drawn to the opportunity to work alongside individuals living with serious mental illness and help them overcome barriers to care through trust, compassion and genuine human connection.

What has kept me connected to firsthand is the people and the opportunity to grow without losing sight of that mission. I began as a community resource guide, later became a senior community resource guide and eventually returned to the company as a training specialist. Even though my role has changed, I’m still contributing to the same purpose, now by preparing and supporting the team members who work directly with the individuals we serve.

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at firsthand Health?

My time at firsthand has helped me recognize that my ability to support people extends beyond direct service. As a community resource guide and senior community resource guide, I strengthened my skills in relationship-building, problem-solving, advocacy and navigating complex situations. I also began mentoring team members, supporting onboarding and sharing practices that helped others feel more confident in their roles.

Those experiences helped me discover a passion for learning and development. In my current role as a training specialist, I’m developing new skills in facilitation, instructional design, learner engagement and evaluating whether training is effective. I’ve grown from focusing primarily on how I can help one individual at a time to thinking about how I can equip an entire team to create meaningful impact.

“I’ve grown from focusing primarily on how I can help one individual at a time to thinking about how I can equip an entire team to create meaningful impact.”

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

Returning to firsthand as a training specialist was the moment that made my growth feel especially clear. I was coming back to help prepare new hires for work that I had once performed myself. I could anticipate the questions new team members might have, explain the realities of the role and connect training concepts to situations I had personally encountered in the field. It was a full-circle moment: I was no longer only applying what I had learned to my own work but was also helping others build the confidence and skills to do theirs well. That experience showed me that my growth could have a ripple effect across the organization and, ultimately, reach the individuals we serve.

Halle Harris Customer Success Manager • Dealerware

Dealerware’s platform is designed to help car dealerships streamline their operations and enhance fleet management.

What originally attracted you to Dealerware, and what has kept you here as you’ve grown in your career?

I have always been a car enthusiast ever since I was a little girl, but I had no perspective of the automotive industry and the massive machine that it is. In college, I was navigating the concept of a lifelong career and what that may look like. I was introduced to someone with a long history in automotive, and she became my mentor, guiding me into the light of the automotive industry. She helped me realize automotive was definitely what I wanted to do. She worked at Dealerware, and I bugged her about it all the time. When an office manager internship came up, she called me and said, “Hey, we just posted this job. You should apply.” And that’s exactly what I did.

Dealerware has always felt like a family. I’ve been very supportive in whatever journey I’ve ever wanted to take. It never felt like the ceiling was too low. As an intern, I made it clear I was here to learn and soak up as much knowledge as I could, and my manager created opportunities for me to shadow individual teams. That feeling of openness never went away. It still feels like that today. If I’m confused, I can go sit in on an engineering meeting, and everyone’s supportive and willing to help me understand.

“As an intern, I made it clear I was here to learn and soak up as much knowledge as I could, and my manager created opportunities for me to shadow individual teams.”

How have you grown or developed professionally during your time at Dealerware?

I started as an intern doing office management. At first, it was this super daunting idea, but it became so much more than a typical office management role. It was really fun, but I quickly wanted more; I wanted to get my hands dirty.

Eventually, I became part of our customer support team. I wasn’t excited about it at first, but it ended up being the role that really transformed me into who I am professionally. It’s the epitome of all the knowledge I currently have, and I think it’s probably one of the hardest jobs at Dealerware. I really appreciate everything I learned. It made me into a sharp tool that can be put into any scenario quickly.

About nine months in, I knew I could solve any problem, and I was ready to be more customer-facing to talk to dealers more. My manager was super supportive of my growth and made it abundantly clear that was what she was there for. After months of those conversations, I finally had the opportunity to apply to the customer success manager team, which was my goal from the beginning. I got it, and it was really fulfilling as an individual to finally reach the role I always envisioned myself in. And that’s what I’m currently doing.

Can you share a moment, project or experience that made you realize how much you’ve grown in your role?

During my time in the support role, there were moments in phone calls where customers would say, “Oh, it’s you, Halle — thank goodness I got you.” That was so fulfilling. It highlighted the relationship aspect, which I always knew I was good at. They remembered my name, even if I didn’t remember who they were. Those calls fueled me. Hearing someone say, “This was so incredibly helpful,” after I walked them through something simple. It could completely change their entire day.

But getting the call about being promoted to customer success manager was the moment. The CSM manager at the time called from a number I didn’t have saved, and I declined it four times. She finally texted me, “This is Jaime. You have to answer my phone call.” I immediately called her, and she said, “You got the job.” That was the most flying-high moment. I was like, this is literally the goal. This was the role where I’d really said, “I don’t know how I’m gonna get there, but that’s it.” It took me about a week to stop crying regularly. It was surreal. That had been my entire goal since I started as an intern.

The stock is currently trading at $6.32, breaking above its 52-week high of $5.49, with a strong three-month return of nearly 20%.

The firm increased its price target to reflect higher revenue growth following Riskified’s increased guidance. The top line outperformance was offset to a large degree by higher chargebacks, resulting in a more measured beat on gross profit.

Goldman Sachs remains cautious on the competitive dynamics for fraud solutions, citing acquirer and network linked solutions and the increased prevalence of liability shifts towards banks in payment methods such as Apple Pay as sources of elevated competition.

The firm identified the potential for prediction markets to be a positive catalyst for Riskified’s stock going forward. The company posted adjusted earnings of $0.02 per share, matching analyst estimates, while revenue reached $98.7 million, surpassing the projected $89.18 million. This marks a 22% increase in revenue from the previous year, representing the fastest growth rate in over four years. Riskified also raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between ILS 400 million and ILS 410 million and adjusted EBITDA guidance to between $33 million and $39 million. # Goldman Sachs raises Riskified stock price target on revenue growth

[Stock Markets](https://uk.investing.com/news/stock-market-news)

Published 12/08/2026, 22:16

Goldman Sachs raises Riskified stock price target on revenue growth

[View all comments (0)0](#comments-4828711)

Goldman Sachs raises Riskified stock price target on revenue growth

[View all comments (0)0](#comments-4828711)

© Credit: Karen Haberberg, Riskified PR

In this article:

[RSKD+19.92%](https://uk.investing.com/equities/riskified)

Investing.com - Goldman Sachs raised its price target on Riskified Ltd. ([NYSE:RSKD](/equities/riskified)) to $5.50 from $4.75 while maintaining a Sell rating on the stock.

The firm cited the company’s sharp acceleration in growth driven by new client signings and leverage to recent sporting events. Goldman Sachs said the market appreciated these factors, leading to significant share outperformance. The stock is currently trading at $6.32, breaking above its 52-week high of $5.49, with a strong three-month return of nearly 20%.

The firm increased its price target to reflect higher revenue growth following Riskified’s increased guidance. The top line outperformance was offset to a large degree by higher chargebacks, resulting in a more measured beat on gross profit.

Goldman Sachs remains cautious on the competitive dynamics for fraud solutions, citing acquirer and network linked solutions and the increased prevalence of liability shifts towards banks in payment methods such as Apple Pay as sources of elevated competition.

The firm identified the potential for prediction markets to be a positive catalyst for Riskified’s stock going forward. Analysts predict the company will turn profitable this year, with revenue growth forecast at 10%. According to [InvestingPro](https://uk.investing.com/pro/RSKD) analysis, the stock appears slightly undervalued at current levels, with a GOOD financial health score. Investors seeking deeper insights can access comprehensive Pro Research Reports covering RSKD and 1,400+ other US equities.

In other recent news, Riskified reported its second-quarter 2026 earnings, which aligned with Wall Street’s profit expectations and exceeded revenue forecasts. The company posted adjusted earnings of $0.02 per share, matching analyst estimates, while revenue reached $98.7 million, surpassing the projected $89.18 million. This marks a 22% increase in revenue from the previous year, representing the fastest growth rate in over four years. Riskified also raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between ILS 400 million and ILS 410 million and adjusted EBITDA guidance to between $33 million and $39 million. The company credited this growth to new business and increased multi-product adoption, with the multi-product merchant base expanding by approximately 50% year over year. Additionally, adjusted EBITDA saw an 84% year-over-year increase to ILS 3.9 million, indicating stronger operating leverage. Management highlighted the complexity of fraud as a driver for demand in its platform, which covers checkout, identity, and dispute management. The quarter was described as an inflection point, with notable new logo wins and broad-based demand across various regions and categories.

Investing.com - Riskified ([NYSE: RSKD](/equities/riskified)) reported second quarter EPS of $0.020, in line with the analyst estimate of $0.020. Revenue for the quarter came in at $98.69M versus the consensus estimate of $89.18M.

## Guidance

Riskified sees FY 2026 revenue of $400.000M-$410.000M versus the analyst consensus of $380.200M.

Riskified’s stock price closed at $5.27. It is up 14.320% in the last 3 months and up 1.540% in the last 12 months.

Riskified saw 0 positive EPS revisions and 2 negative EPS revisions in the last 90 days. See Riskified’s stock price’s past reactions to earnings [here](https://www.investing.com/pro/INVESTING:1175354/earnings).

Investing.com - U.S. stock futures edged higher on Wednesday, as investors awaited key consumer inflation data that could provide fresh clues on the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate path, while a string of corporate earnings updates drove sharp moves in individual stocks.

[**Get full insights on U.S. premarket movers with InvestingPro - now 55% off**](https://in.investing.com/pro/landing-page)

By 06:24 ET (10:24 GMT), the [Dow](/indices/us-30) futures contract had risen by 62 points, or 0.1%, S&P 500 futures had gained 22 points, or 0.3%, and [Nasdaq 100](/indices/nq-100-futures) futures had climbed 217 points, or 0.7%.

The inflation report will be closely watched by investors assessing the timing and scale of potential Fed rate cuts. A softer-than-expected reading could reinforce expectations for lower borrowing costs, while a hotter print could put pressure on rate-sensitive technology stocks.

Here are some of the biggest premarket U.S. stock movers today:

[Super Micro Computer](/equities/super-micro-compu) shares rallied more than 9% before the bell after the AI server maker issued full-year financial guidance that came in well above Wall Street expectations.

The upbeat outlook helped ease concerns following the company’s preliminary July update, which had pointed to softer-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue. Investors are now focusing on whether strong demand for AI infrastructure can translate into sustained growth for the company.

H&R Block shares surged 13.9% in premarket trading after the tax preparation company reported better-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings and issued a stronger-than-anticipated outlook.

Adjusted EPS for the quarter ended June 30 came in at $2.38, above the $2.31 analyst consensus. Full-year adjusted EPS rose 13.9% to $5.31, while revenue increased 4.9% to $3.95 billion.

For fiscal 2027, H&R Block forecast adjusted EPS of $6.04 to $6.24. The midpoint is roughly 4.8% above previous analyst expectations, suggesting investors see scope for the company’s strategy to deliver more durable earnings growth.

[Owlet](/equities/sandbridge-acquisition) stock jumped nearly 10% before the open after the digital parenting platform reported record second-quarter results.

Revenue rose 29.9% year-over-year to $33.9 million, while its adjusted loss narrowed to just $0.01 per share, substantially better than the $0.10 loss analysts had expected.

The stock had already gained about 5.8% after hours on Tuesday, with the momentum carrying into Wednesday’s premarket session.

[Valens Semiconductor](/equities/ptk-acquisition) shares climbed 14.9% after the chipmaker reported second-quarter revenue of $18.1 million and raised its full-year revenue outlook.

Revenue increased 6.1% from a year earlier and exceeded the company’s own guidance of $17.2 million to $17.6 million, although it was marginally below the $18.13 million analyst consensus.

The stronger full-year outlook nevertheless gave investors a reason to look beyond the modest quarterly miss.

[Riskified](/equities/riskified) shares rose 15.8% before the bell after the e-commerce fraud prevention company reported its strongest revenue growth in more than four years.

Second-quarter revenue jumped 22% year-over-year to $98.7 million, comfortably exceeding the $89.2 million analyst consensus. Adjusted EPS of $0.02 matched expectations, while free cash flow reached $12.9 million.

The acceleration in revenue growth is likely to be the key focus for investors as the company continues to build out its fraud-prevention platform.

[Annexon](/equities/annexon-inc) shares fell 5.9% in premarket trading after the company amended its Phase 3 ARCHER II trial of vonaprument for dry age-related macular degeneration with geographic atrophy.

The amendment adds a month-24 co-primary endpoint alongside the original month-15 assessment, allowing the study to meet its primary objective at either timepoint.

The change has raised concerns among investors that the month-15 data may not provide a sufficiently clear efficacy signal. The company is still expected to report topline results in the fourth quarter of 2026.

# Why is Riskified stock surging today?

Editor[Maria Ponnezhath](https://za.investing.com/members/contributors/264622975)

[Stock Markets](https://za.investing.com/news/stock-market-news)

Why is Riskified stock surging today?

[View all comments (0)0](#comments-4423980)

Why is Riskified stock surging today?

[View all comments (0)0](#comments-4423980)

© Reuters

In this article:

[RSKD+19.92%](https://za.investing.com/equities/riskified)

Investing.com -- [Riskified](/equities/riskified) stock surged 15.8% in pre-open trading after the ecommerce fraud prevention company published its second-quarter 2026 financial results before the market opened, revealing revenue of $98.7 million — a 22% year-over-year jump that marked the company’s strongest top-line growth in over four years and came in well ahead of the analyst consensus estimate of $89.2 million.

Adjusted earnings per share of $0.02 met expectations, while free cash flow reached $12.9 million during the quarter.

Equally important to investors was the company’s decision to raise its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $400–$410 million, with a midpoint of $405 million that significantly exceeded the prior Wall Street consensus of approximately $380 million — representing the second guidance increase of the year.

CEO Eido Gal pointed to accelerating new business momentum and a broadening multi-product customer base as the drivers, while CFO Aglika Dotcheva highlighted the company’s strong balance sheet and improving profitability as giving management the confidence to continue investing in the platform while returning capital to shareholders through its buyback program.

The broader U.S. equity market provided a constructive backdrop for the move, with the S&P 500 adding 0.3%, the Nasdaq gaining 0.7%, and the Dow Jones edging up 0.1%, reflecting a generally risk-on environment that amplified investor enthusiasm for a high-growth fintech name delivering a meaningful positive earnings surprise.

The stock’s pre-market price of $6.10 also pushed it decisively above its previous 52-week high of $5.485, a technical breakout that may attract additional momentum-driven interest once the regular session opens.

Taken together, the combination of a substantial revenue beat, a raised full-year outlook, healthy free cash flow, and an accommodating market backdrop created a powerful catalyst for today’s outsized move, reinforcing the bull case that Riskified’s AI-powered fraud intelligence platform is gaining meaningful traction with merchants at scale.

data.title: Riskified Reports Strong Second Quarter of 2026 with Accelerating Revenue Growth
data.ai_summary: Riskified reported a 22% year-over-year revenue increase to $98.7 million for the second quarter of 2026, marking its strongest growth in over four years driven by new merchant acquisitions and upselling activity. The company raised its full-year revenue guidance to between $400 million and $410 million and increased Adjusted EBITDA projections following improved profitability metrics and strong free cash flow generation.

Riskified Reports Strong Second Quarter of 2026 with Accelerating Revenue Growth Published at August 12th 2026, 6:45 AM EDT via Business Wire ⓘ This article is third-party content and does not represent the views of this site. We make no guarantees regarding its accuracy or completeness. Raises Revenue and Adjusted EBITDA guidance Riskified Ltd. (NYSE: RSKD) (the “Company”, “Riskified”, “we” or “our”), a leader in ecommerce fraud and risk intelligence, today announced financial results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026. The Company will host an investor call to discuss these results today at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time. "We delivered our strongest revenue growth in over four years, driven by increasingly complex fraud and merchant demand for the unified platform we've spent years building. That's showing up in accelerating new business and a deepening multi-product base, and it's why we're raising our outlook for the second time this year," said Eido Gal, CEO & Co-Founder of Riskified. Q2 2026 and Recent Business Highlights Strongest Revenue Growth in Over Four Years: Revenue grew 22% year-over-year to $98.7 million, an acceleration from 7% growth in the first quarter, driven by continued new merchant and upsell activity.

Accelerating New Business Momentum: New logo acquisition was a significant contributor to results this quarter. Continued ACH and Non-Card Expansion: Our investment in ACH-specific models and features extended our broader payments capabilities, with ACH becoming a meaningful and growing part of new business this quarter. The dollar value of ACH transactions that Riskified processed in the quarter was approximately 19 times higher than the value processed in the second quarter of the prior year.

"We delivered robust revenue growth in the second quarter, with continued expansion in Adjusted EBITDA," said Aglika Dotcheva, Chief Financial Officer of Riskified. "Revenue grew 22% year-over-year to $98.7 million, accelerating from 7% growth in the first quarter, and Adjusted EBITDA increased 84% to $3.9 million. We also generated $12.9 million in free cash flow while returning capital to shareholders through our buyback program. Our strong balance sheet and improving profitability give us the confidence and flexibility to keep investing in the platform while raising our full-year outlook." Financial Outlook For the year ending December 31, 2026: We now anticipate revenue to be between $400 million and $410 million, or $405 million to the midpoint, up from our prior range of between $376 million and $384 million. This reflects the flow-through of our second quarter revenue outperformance, as well as an incremental raise to our outlook based on the momentum we are seeing in the business. We now anticipate Adjusted EBITDA to be between $33 million and $39 million, or $36 million to the midpoint, up from our prior range of $28 million to $34 million. The primary factors that may determine where we fall within each range are consistent with what we shared last quarter - the timing and ramping of new merchant go-lives and existing merchant upsells, our success in retaining our merchants, and the broader macro environment. (1) GMV is a key performance indicator. See “Key Performance Indicators and Non-GAAP Measures” for additional information and “Reconciliation of GAAP to Non-GAAP Measures” for a reconciliation to the most directly comparable GAAP measure. (2) We refer to certain forward-looking non-GAAP financial measures in this press release and on our quarterly results conference call. We are not able to provide a reconciliation of forward-looking Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA margin, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross profit margin, non-GAAP operating expense, or free cash flow for the fiscal year ending December 31, 2026 to net profit (loss), gross profit, total operating expenses, and operating cash flow, respectively, because certain items that are excluded from these non-GAAP metrics but included in the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures, cannot be predicted on a forward-looking basis without unreasonable effort or are not within our control. For example, we are unable to forecast the magnitude of foreign currency transaction gains or losses which are subject to many economic and other factors beyond our control. For the same reasons, we are unable to address the probable significance of the unavailable information, which could have a potentially unpredictable and significant impact on our future GAAP financial results. Conference Call and Webcast Details The Company will host a conference call to discuss its financial results today, August 12, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time. A live webcast of the call can be accessed from Riskified’s Investor Relations website at ir.riskified.com. A replay of the webcast will also be available for a limited time at ir.riskified.com. The press release with the financial results, as well as the investor presentation materials will also be accessible on the Company’s Investor Relations website prior to the conference call. Key Performance Indicators and Non-GAAP Measures This press release and the accompanying tables contain references to Gross Merchandise Volume ("GMV"), which is a key performance indicator, and to certain non-GAAP measures which include non-GAAP measures of financial performance such as Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted EBITDA margin, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP gross profit margin, non-GAAP cost of revenue, non-GAAP operating expenses by line item, non-GAAP constant currency operating expenses, non-GAAP net profit (loss), and non-GAAP net profit (loss) per share, and a non-GAAP measure of liquidity, Free Cash Flow. Management and our Board of Directors use key performance indicators and non-GAAP measures as supplemental measures of performance and liquidity because they assist us in comparing our operating performance on a consistent basis, as they remove the impact of items that we believe do not directly reflect our core operations. We also use Adjusted EBITDA for planning purposes, including the preparation of our internal annual operating budget and financial projections, to evaluate the performance and effectiveness of our strategic initiatives, and to evaluate our capacity to expand our business. Free Cash Flow provides useful information to management and investors about the amount of cash generated by the business that can be used for strategic opportunities, including investing in our business and strengthening our balance sheet. These non-GAAP measures should not be construed as an inference that our future results will be unaffected by unusual or other items. Non-GAAP measures of financial performance have limitations as analytical tools in that these measures do not reflect our cash expenditures, or future requirements for capital expenditures, or contractual commitments; these measures do not reflect changes in, or cash requirements for, our working capital needs; these measures do not reflect our tax expense or the cash requirements to pay our taxes, and assets being depreciated and amortized will often have to be replaced in the future and these measures do not reflect any cash requirements for such replacements. Non-GAAP constant currency operating expenses is limited because it reflects a hypothetical recalculation of operating expenses using prior-period exchange rates and therefore does not reflect the actual operating expenses incurred by the business or the economic impact of foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations on our results, which are inherent to our global operations. Free Cash Flow is limited because it does not represent the residual cash flow available for discretionary expenditures. Free Cash Flow is not necessarily a measure of our ability to fund our cash needs. In light of these limitations, management uses these non-GAAP measures to supplement, not replace, our GAAP results. The non-GAAP measures used herein are not necessarily comparable to similarly titled captions of other companies due to different calculation methods. Non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation, as an alternative to, or superior to information prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP. These measures are frequently used by analysts, investors and other interested parties to evaluate companies in our industry. By providing these non-GAAP measures together with a reconciliation to the most comparable GAAP measure, we believe we are enhancing investors' understanding of our business and our results of operations, as well as assisting investors in evaluating how well we are executing our strategic initiatives. We define GMV as the gross total dollar value of orders reviewed through our AI fraud and risk intelligence platform during the period indicated, including the value of orders that we did not approve. GMV is an indicator of the success of our merchants and the scale of our platform. GMV does not represent transactions successfully completed on our merchants’ websites or revenue earned by us, however, our revenue is directionally correlated with the level of GMV reviewed through our platform and is an indicator of future revenue opportunities. We generate revenue based on the portion of GMV we approve multiplied by the associated risk-adjusted fee. We define each of our non-GAAP measures of financial performance, as the respective GAAP balances shown in the below tables, adjusted for, as applicable, depreciation and amortization (including amortization of capitalized internal-use software as presented in our statement of cash flows), share-based compensation expense, payroll taxes related to share-based compensation, legal-related and other expenses, restructuring costs, provision for (benefit from) income taxes, other income (expense) including foreign currency transaction gains and losses and gains and losses on non-designated hedges, and interest income (expense). Adjusted EBITDA margin represents Adjusted EBITDA expressed as a percentage of revenue. Non-GAAP Gross Profit Margin represents Non-GAAP Gross Profit expressed as a percentage of revenue. We define non-GAAP net profit (loss) per share as non-GAAP net profit (loss) divided by non-GAAP weighted-average shares. We define non-GAAP weighted-average shares, as GAAP weighted average shares, adjusted to reflect any dilutive ordinary share equivalents resulting from non-GAAP net profit (loss), if applicable. We define non-GAAP constant currency operating expenses as total non-GAAP operating expenses excluding the impact of our hedging program and foreign exchange rate movements. We use it to determine the impact that exchange rate changes have on our results. Non-GAAP constant currency operating expenses is calculated by translating current period non-GAAP operating expenses excluding hedging gains/losses using the prior period exchange rate. We define Free Cash Flow as net cash provided by (used in) operating activities, less cash purchases of property and equipment and capitalized software development costs. Management believes that by excluding certain items from the associated GAAP measure, these non-GAAP measures are useful in assessing our performance and provide meaningful supplemental information due to the following factors: Depreciation and amortization: We exclude depreciation and amortization (including amortization of capitalized internal-use software) because we believe that these costs are not core to the performance of our business and the utilization of the underlying assets being depreciated and amortized can change without a corresponding impact on the operating performance of our business. Management believes that excluding depreciation and amortization facilitates comparability with other companies in our industry. Share-based compensation expense: We exclude share-based compensation expense primarily because it is a non-cash expense that does not directly correlate to the current performance of our business. This is partly because the expense is calculated based on the grant date fair value of an award which may vary significantly from the current fair market value of the award based on factors outside of our control. Share-based compensation expense is principally aimed at aligning our employees’ interests with those of our shareholders and at long-term retention, rather than to address operational performance for any particular period. Payroll taxes related to share-based compensation: We exclude employer payroll tax expense related to share-based compensation in order to see the full effect that excluding that share-based compensation expense had on our operating results. These expenses are tied to the exercise or vesting of underlying equity awards and the price of our common stock at the time of vesting or exercise, which may vary from period to period independent of the operating performance of our business. Legal-related and other expenses: We exclude certain costs incurred in connection with corporate initiatives that are non-recurring and not reflective of costs associated with our ongoing business and operating results and are viewed as unusual and infrequent. Restructuring costs: We exclude costs associated with reductions in force because these costs are related to one-time severance and benefit payments and are not reflective of costs associated with our ongoing business and operating results and are viewed as unusual and infrequent. See the tables below for reconciliations of these non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures. Adds StockTitan as a preferred source · opens Google Add on Google Not now 12/08/2026 - 03:45 Raises Revenue and Adjusted EBITDA guidance NEW YORK --(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Riskified Ltd. (NYSE: RSKD) (the “Company”, “Riskified”, “we” or “our”), a leader in ecommerce fraud and risk intelligence, today announced financial results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2026. The Company will host an investor call to discuss these results today at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time. "We delivered our strongest revenue growth in over four years, driven by increasingly complex fraud and merchant demand for the unified platform we've spent years building. That's showing up in accelerating new business and a deepening multi-product base, and it's why we're raising our outlook for the second time this year," said Eido Gal, CEO & Co-Founder of Riskified. Q2 2026 and Recent Business Highlights Strongest Revenue Growth in Over Four Years: Revenue grew 22% year-over-year to $98.7 million , an acceleration from 7% growth in the first quarter, driven by continued new merchant and upsell activity.

Accelerating New Business Momentum: New logo acquisition was a significant contributor to results this quarter. We added new logos across all four regions, with five of our top ten headquartered outside the United States , spanning five categories.

Sustained Competitive Win Rates: Our competitive win rates remained above 75% in the second quarter, reflecting the differentiation of our platform compared to alternatives that merchants consider.

Our competitive win rates remained above in the second quarter, reflecting the differentiation of our platform compared to alternatives that merchants consider. Continued ACH and Non-Card Expansion: Our investment in ACH-specific models and features extended our broader payments capabilities, with ACH becoming a meaningful and growing part of new business this quarter. The dollar value of ACH transactions that Riskified processed in the quarter was approximately 19 times higher than the value processed in the second quarter of the prior year.

The dollar value of ACH transactions that Riskified processed in the quarter was approximately 19 times higher than the value processed in the second quarter of the prior year. Platform Expansion: Merchants are increasingly using Riskified’s identity intelligence beyond checkout to improve the customer experience across the transaction lifecycle. Our AI assistant, ARIA, continued to gain traction this quarter. We have embedded ARIA across our wider platform, giving fraud and risk teams a highly effective tool that helps them investigate activity, understand emerging trends, and take action more quickly.

Our AI assistant, ARIA, continued to gain traction this quarter. We have embedded ARIA across our wider platform, giving fraud and risk teams a highly effective tool that helps them investigate activity, understand emerging trends, and take action more quickly. Live Sports Driving Category Momentum: A dense global events calendar, including the World Cup and NBA Finals, drove elevated volumes across Tickets and Digital Finance.
